I move to add the words at the end of that sub-clause ' or is within the limit of deviation allowed under this Act.'

speechtext: Why do you insert these words ?
Because we have already passed a clause which allows a deviation of 100 yards if the board approves.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This gives two alternatives; one that the land shall be required for the railway and the other that it shall be within the limit of deviation. Would not the expression ' is required for the railway ' cover everything ? It is of no importance whatever that it is within the limit of deviation unless it is required for the railway.

Under the Act the deviation may be allowed by the board without requiring that they should file plans, and if

within the limits of deviation more land is required, they could be allowed to take it without going through all the formalities necessary to secure the right of way in the first place.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It seems to me that we should not use any language which enables a certificate to be given merely because land happens to be within the range of deviation. You cannot take it without some authority given in the Act, and yet you put that language in as an alternative cla.use to the other.

Although the words are left out in the Bill as submitted, these words are found in section 147 of the existing Act. In conference with the legal gentlemen who represent the various railway companies and who have given me the benefit of their views with regard to many of the clauses, they expressed a strong opinion that we had better restore the language of the old Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I can understand that legal gentlemen representing the railway companies should want these words in because the railway company gets the whole benefit. It would not be necessary with these words in the Act, that the lands be required for the railway, but only that they should be within the limit of deviation. Although there might be a serious question as to whether the railway really required the land, yet they would contend that as it was within the limits, the onus was taken off them. Although It is presupposed that the board will not allow them to enter on this 300 feet deviation unless they think it necessary, yet they might say that the alternative was given and that they could take the land because it is within the limits of the deviation, just as well as If they needed it for the railway. Unless it is really absolutely necessary for the railway, they should not be allowed to cut into a private owner's property. We must not allow the landowner to hold up the railway company, but, on the other hand, we must not allow the railway company to hold up the landowner. Because the railway company had a right to take one part of a man's land, it might wantonly take another part which it did not require for the purposes of the railway. Sometimes directors of railway companies are interested in other ventures besides railways; and if they could, by virtue of using their rights as a railway company, make the landowner give land which was not needed for the railway, they might work serious injustice to the landowner. I would suggest that the word ' aud ' be used instead of the word * or.' That would be my second choice, but my first choice would be to insert the words ' on the terms permitted by this Act.'

The section does limit them. It
is not the case that the railway company is allowed, on its own free will, and without the sanction or authority of the board, to take anybody's lands in the form of a deviation. The bon. gentleman will remember that the board is vested with jurisdiction for such purposes. This clause does not make provision for the taking of the land, but simply provides what the notice shall contain. I do not think it would help matters to substitute the word * and ' for the word ' or.' This language is in the existing law, and I do not think it has occasioned any difficulty or is likely to leave the way open to any serious outrages.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

On section 161-compensation for lands and damage.

I propose to substitute for section 161 the following :
The arbitrator or arbitrators, in deciding on such value or compensation, shall take into consideration the increased value that will be given to any lands through or over which the railway will pass, by reason of the passage of the railway through or over the same, or by reason of the construction of the railway, and shall set off the increased value that will attach to the said lands or grounds, against the inconvenience, loss or damage that might be suffered or sustained by reason of the company taking possession of or using the said lands as aforesaid.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is the wording in tlie old Act ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
While that is being discussed, I have an amendment which I

intended to propose to the section as it appeared in the Bill, hut it will be applicable to this amended section, except that the lining will be different. This is an important matter, and I think I had better mention the amendment I propose and explain the reason for it, in order that the minister may consider it, and, if he agrees with me incorporate it in the Bill. There are two sorts of increases in value that appertain to lands taken for railway purposes. First there is the increase of value common to the whole locality due to the construction of the railway and the opening up of the section of country it traverses. The second is a special increase and is involved also in the existing law, which the minister proposes to re-enact.
But, I am sorry to say that in the province of Ontario the judges do not agree on what the law means. The best opinion- if I may say so ; I mean what seems to me the best opinion-is in accordance with what I attempt to make clear by my amendment ; and that is that no farmer or other owner of property shall be charged, as a set off against the damages to which he is subject, with any increase in the value of his land which increase is common to himself and others by reason of the construction of the railway, but only such increased value as attaches to his land and not to neighbouring land. The late Chief Justice Burton was strongly of opinion that the law is as I have suggested by my amendment to make it.
That is not the recognized law.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
No, I am sorry to say it is not, and that is why I am going to make it safe in this Act, so that people having these cases may not have an appeal from the arbitrators. I have had perhaps as much experience as any lawyer in Ontario of my age with regard to these railway arbitrations. I have lately been an arbitrator, as well as counsel in such cases for fifteen or twenty years, and I have found many a time there was an appeal owing to the disagreement of the arbitrators and coming down from the price it was really thought the man would be entitled to, because they could not otherwise agree upon what they thought the law was as to what was to be set off. The late chief Justice Burton was strongly of the opinion that the law was as it is made by my amendment, that it meant what I am saying now, that the man should not be charged against the damages to which he was clearly entitled any set-off for increased values to his remaining land which value was common also to his neighbours. But other judges have not agreed with him, and I find arbitrators, among whom are county judges and lawyers of good ability, disagreeing on that point. I had the misfortune to sit upon an arbitration myself in
Hamilton, where the arbitrators had to disagree; they could not agree whether they should allow as a set-off for damages the benefit the party received for the increased value of the rest of his land when that value was common to his neighbours, because, it was argued, that man could get to market quicker, he can ship fruit easier, and so on. But it was stated on the other hand, well, but that is a benefit common to his neighbours who do not give any land, and there the arbitrators, I am sorry to say, were not able to agree upon how they should put that point. I think we ought to make it clear, and that a man should not be charged with the benefit to his property against the damages which he suffered through the passing of a railway across his land, unless it is a special benefit not common to every one. If the minister does not agree with me, I am prepared to debate the point at considerable length, that a man should not be charged against for any increased value unless it is the value special to him over that which his neighbours receive.

I would like to hear the opinion of the leader of the opposition on this question. I do not know that the proposition will strike the committee favourably. I am under the impression that in my own province the law is generally accepted as stated by the hon. member for Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster). I would be inclined to accept the amendment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am not familiar with Ontario decisions on the point. The idea in my mind was, how would you deal in that case along similar lines with the inconvenience, loss and damages to the lands traversed ? I have no particular case in mind, but the general principle is that a man can recover damages where his lands have been taken, or some of his lands. Then he can also recover damages in respect to other lands not taken but being part of the same lot ? That is to say, you may have two lots side by side, one lot owned by A and another lot owned by B. Taking into consideration the detriment which is occasioned to the land of A because a portion of his land has been taken, you take into consideration the circumstances affecting the value of that land as a whole; whereas the land of B immediately adjoining may be affected in the same way, but you cannot grant him any compensation at all because no land is taken. My hon. friend from Lincoln wishes to put the man whose land is taken on the same basis as every one else, in respect of increase to the value of his land. But how are you to deal with the corresponding principle. All the community alongside of you is affected exactly in the same way as you are, so far as detriment is concerned, and if you are to be put on the same plane as every one else with re-

gard to advantage, are you not to be put on tlie same plane as every one else with regard to detriment ? It seems to me if you are to equalize the question of advantage you ought also to equalize the question of damage. The object of my hon. friend's amendment is to say that a man whose land is taken must not suffer any reduction of the price on account of increased advantage if all his neighbours have an exactly similar advantage to that which he receives. If the principle is good to that extent should not the converse be good.

I think the arbitrators have generally proceeded upon the principle that a man whose lands are not taken by the railway dees not, in the case put by my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax), sustain quite the same damages. It is the severance of a man's farm that creates the trouble. If a man's lands are not taken by the railway they are not severed at all. In the abstract, as put by my hon. friend, it appears to be one and the same question, but It does not work out iu that way once in a hundred times as a matter of fact. The man whose lands are not taken is not damaged because they are not severed. The railway does not cut him off from his woods or his pasture field, it does not run between his house and his barn or his house and the highway, and therefore it does not damage the remainder of his land. The man who is not damaged has all the advantage of the railway running there and perhaps a greater advantage than the man whose lands are taken because he is almost as near to the station as the man whose lands are taken, and he does not sustain any damage by the severance. I do not therefore think he is in a position to say that the other man is getting more than is given to him when he gets his damages in respect to the severance.

The illustration the hon. minister referred to a moment ago is on the same principle. The Intercolonial Railway was running along Water street in the city of Halifax. The railway went along that street under the terms of a special statute enabling the highway to be used for that purpose and also by permission of the corporation of the city of Halifax. It took up one half of the street from the curb, the result of it being that the land on the other side of the street was reduced in value by at least 50 per cent and some of it by 75 per cent. The people went to the Exchequer Court and they could not recover a dollar. I think that is what the Exchequer Couft held, although it may be that their petition was dismissed by that court under the statute of limitations. I think that is what the court would have decided in any case. If the land of one of these proprietors had extended across the street there would Mr. BORDER (Halifax),
have been a different condition of affairs under which the man who owned this land which had been taken would not only have had damages for the land so taken, but damages for the injury to buildings on the other side of the street ; whereas, this land did not extend across the street, the land was not taken and the owners had no status in the court at all. 1 think in all fairness from one standpoint that the amendment which my hon. friend from Lincoln and Niagara suggests has something commendable in it, but I would like to see whether or not, if you are going to amend the law, you could not adopt some principle which would deal in an equitable manner with the converse condition. I suppose from the standpoint of the public it would be the fairest not to regard the principle which has prevailed in the past, that damages cannot be recovered unless the land is taken, but I suspect that it would be very difficult for the railway company to know just where matters were going to end if a principle of that kind in respect of line through any thickly settled district were adopted. You remember the question which arose in New York when the elevated road was constructed. Damages were recovered on account of vibration and everything of that kind and the litigation extended over many years. I think the amendment of my hon. friend is well worthy of the serious attention of the committee, but we had perhaps better think of it a little before adopting it.

I would be very reluctant to undertake to make any material changes in the principle upon which the courts have been acting heretofore in respect to these valuations. We would not know where we might land ourselves. A very long course of judicial interpretation as well as of legislation throughout the English speaking countries, I think, has pretty well synchronized in a uniform way, and I would not care to take the responsibility just now, when dealing with this Bill, to make what might be thought to be a progressive movement. I would feel like agreeing to my hon. friend's amendment to-day, because it seems to me to be in accord with the doctrine which obtains generally in our courts, if it were not a departure. I should like to have an opportunity to consider it, and I think I would prefer not dealing with it in this form, but defer consideration until some later session when we might deal with the subject separately.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is not intended as a departure. I do not think it has that effect.

If it were felt to be desirable to make some provision to meet the case which the hon. leader of the opposition has

referred to, we would find it a very large undertaking. These things ramify in such extreme directions that we cannot anticipate where they are going to carry us. We cannot establish uniformity any way. I think, that, having gone as far as we have, we ought to stop. I would agree that the words should be added if the committee approve the amendment which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) proposes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think it is dangerous to alter the wording of the Act as it is. The only advantage which the landowner whose land is taken can have over another neighbour is better access to the station and better drainage for his land on account of the passage of a railway over it. These advantages are allowed at present and changing the wording of the Act would lead to confusion.

I quite agree with the member for Lanark that drainage and access to a station are the two things that are generally brought forward. I know where it has worked hardly with the landowners, because in order to get the award of two of the arbitrators there has had to be a compromise which would not have been the case, if it were established what their rights were.

The amendment proposed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) is within reasonable limits, and I think it would meet the difficulty. No deduction should be made from compensation because of benefits from the passage of a railway that are common to all the lands in the neighbourhood.
Would this amendment have the effect of preventing compensation being given to other lands, not taken by the railway which are not damaged.

It does not affect them at all. I move that section 161 be stricken out and the following substituted :
The arbitrators or arbitrator in deciding on such value or compensation shall take into consideration the increased value which will be given to any lands through or over which the railway will pass by reason of the passage of the railway through or over the same, or by reason of the construction of the railway, and shall set off such increased value that will attach to the said lands or grounds against the inconvenience loss or damage that may be suffered or sustained by reason of the company taking possession of or using the said lands as aforesaid.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I beg to move to amend the section by inserting after the words ' increased value ' the following words : ' beyond the increased value common to all lands in the locality.'
Section, as amended, agreed to.

On section 169, subsection 2, appeal from award,

I move to add after the number two at the very beginning of the section, the words ' whenever the award exceeds $1,000.' The present law limits these appeals to amounts exceeding $400, but this Bill strikes out the limitation and allows an appeal in any case, no matter how small may be the award. The old Act provides a limit of $400, but in my opinion, we should not allow an appeal except in cases where the award is over $1,000. As my hon. friend from Elgin (Mr. Robinson) said, the expenses of arbitration are considerable, and by the time the three arbitrators have come to a conclusion they know pretty well all about the case and what the damages really are. I may be a little influenced by the fact that the landowner can stand an appeal less easily than the railway. A railway company, having an award of $500 or $600 against it, might worry the landowner into accepting $200 or $300 rather than have an appeal. The costs of an arbitration, which he cannot collect from the company, are considerable. What he can collect are the witness fees and the arbitrators' and other fees, which are principally disbursements, but he gets a very small portion of what he has to pay his counsel for preparing his case. And if the railway company should take the case to appeal to the court in Toronto, the landowner must have the case argued over again, and the appeal may go against him or the amount be reduced, and in any case he will be considerably out of pocket. Even if the appeal should be dismissed with costs against the railway, the landowner would not be able to get as much as he would have had if there had been no appeal, because there is a large amount of work which the lawyers have to do and for which they cannot charge in the bill of costs against the company. I think, therefore, that if the award do not exceed a thousand dollars, the railway company should not be allowed to bring it into review. I first thought of making the amount twice as large, but on reflection I thought that the amount of $1,000 would be more acceptable to the House. If the award of the arbitrators is not more than $1,000 against the railway company, selected as the arbitrators are by this Act as arranged by the minister-an arrangement with regard to most of which I entirely agree-I think there can be little doubt that that award will be substantially just, and that to allow an appeal would be inadvisable. For, if an appeal from the award is allowed in the case of say $800, the owner may be persuaded that it is better to take $600 or even $700 than to face the expense of an appeal. He is forced to

take it, not because the law obliges him to, but because he feels it would be more profitable to him in the end. In some cases property owners are inclined to regard this almost as a species of blackmail. The agent of the railway company says :	We
can make you pay a great deal out of this award, if you do not accept a reduction. And so, as the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) said, the farmer is compelled to sustain a loss which he ought not to be called upon to sustain. I submit with confidence that the line should be drawn at $1,000.

The difference that arises is as to the amount. I had intended to suggest that the minimum should be something less than $1,000. I confess that I did not view it as the hon. member (Mr. Lancaster) does, entirely as a question' of appeal on the part of the railway company. I think we may very well consider that either party or both parties may be dissatisfied with the award and may desire to have the subject reviewed. If we are to view1 it as the hon. gentleman does, I think I would be prepared to go as far as he proposes. But are we justified in so doing ? I have not had great experience with respect to these matters, not nearly so much as the hon. member has had. Therefore, I should be very much disposed to be influenced by his views. If we are to take for granted that in only a very small percentage of cases are these valuations complained of by the landowners, and in the great majority of cases by the railway company, I am prepared to say that the amount should be a good deal larger than I had in mind, and I do not say I would not be willing to make it as high as $1,000. It might be well, perhaps, to consider the point further. Where lands are being taken for railway purposes in country districts, one would hardly find one instance in fifty, I suppose, in which the valuation would run as high as $1,000. The effect of this, therefore, would be to allow no appeal in the great majority of cases. I do not think that would be a serious objection. I am. quite sure that the tribunal referred to would be likely to reach a fair result, so far as the farmer is concerned, and I would not be particularly sensitive with regard to the other. Of course, I would not like to see any system which would be manifestly likely to result in gross injustice to the company. They are entitled to fair treatment, and, of course, we depend on the arbitrators, one of whom is to be named by the railway company, to do what is reasonable and just. I think this clause may stand as it is for the present.
On section 169, subsection 3-practice and proceedings on appeal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
This subsection provided :
Upon such appeal the practice and proceedings shall be, as nearly as may be, the same as upon an appeal from the decision of an inferior court to the said court, subject to any general rules or orders from time to time made by the said last mentioned court, in respect to such appeals, which orders may amongst other things provide that any such appeal may be heard and determined by a single judge.
I have an amendment to propose, a copy of which I have just submitted to the hon. minister. When I drew this amendment I assumed that the meaning of 'court' there was the Superior Court. Of course, I do not pretend that they should appeal to the county court. This subsection treats the award of the arbitrators as the decision of an inferior court. Now, speaking for the province of Ontario-and I think the same applies in other provinces-you never appeal from any court to a single judge. The present law in that respect says, among other things, that the court may provide that appeals shall be determined by a single judge. That is the principle I am assailing. My contention is that no one judge, I care not who he may be, should set aside, upon law and fact the decision of three arbitrators in which at least two must have agreed. There is no other case within my knowledge of the courts, where one judge can do that. It is a bad principle, and it does not work wellspeaking for the province of Ontario-in these arbitrations with railway companies. This appeal in railway arbitration is wider than the ordinary appeal. Speaking as a lawyer, I think the appeal from an inferior court is not to be set aside as easily as an award can be. The award here can be set aside if the court determining that appeal think the judge erred on the question of fact, or on the weight of evidence, or the weight to be attached to either class of witnesses. Now, those liabilities to attack do not exist in the ordinary jurisdiction of an appellate court. The law at present is that one single judge can do more than is the result of an appeal from an inferior court. He is allowed, upon a hearing of an appeal, the same power as in the case of original jurisdiction. That is, the court has a right to read the evidence over without seeing the witnesses in the box, or hearing their manner of giving evidence, which properly guides the lower court. The appellate judge can disregard all that, and determine from the written evidence just as if he was accorded original jurisdiction. Now. on principle, I do not think it is right that one judge should have all these wide powers to set aside a decision on a question of fact as well as on a question of law. There is no other appeal, so far as I know, from a lower court, at least in the province of Ontario, that is heard and determined by a single judge.
The Exchequer Court judge.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: His is an inferior court, and a party can appeal from him to the Supreme Court of Canada.

I may say to the hon. gentleman at once, to save him the trouble of arguing at greater length, that I think I would entertain his suggestion. But instead of providing that the appeal can be dealt with by one judge, I would provide that such appeal should be to a Superior Court judge.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: To which of the courts of appeal would you appeal to ? To the divisional court or the court of appeal ?

The Act says that upon such appeal the practice and proceedings shall be as near as may be the same as upon an appeal from an inferior court to the superior court. In Ontario that is to a divisional court. In Ontario the appeal goes to the divisional court of the high court of justice, because the high court of justice is a superior court.
Under the practice in Ontario and under the rules, an appeal can go either to a divisional court or to a court of appeal.
Not from a county court.

Yes, the section provides that the superior court can make and change the rules whereby an appeal from the board of arbitrators, in cases of the appraisement of land taken for railway purposes, can be to a single judge ; but unless the superior court in the province of Ontario, and I apprehend in the other provinces as well, makes an order different from any order that exists at present, there can be no appeal except to a divisional court.
We do not appeal to a single judge in these arbitrations. There has been a standing rule of the high court for ten or twelve years, under which all these appeals do now go to a single judge.

This is a section altogether different from the section in the general Railway Act, which says that upon such an appeal the practice and proceedings shall be as near as may be the same as upon an appeal from the decision of an inferior court. Now, the practice and proceedings at present, on an appeal from an inferior to a superior court, are that the appeal shall be either to the divisional court or to the court of appeal. You appeal from the county court to the divisional court, and from the divisional court to the court of appeal.
You appeal from the county court to the divisional court and from the divisional court to the court of appeal.
Not in a county court. You are limited to one appeal.

I quite admit that. We understand the practice in Ontario as well as the hon. gentleman. Under the provisions of the subsection the practice in an appeal from the board of arbitrators would be exactly similar to the present practice in an appeal from an inferior to a superior court in the province of Ontario, and that is either the divisional court or the court of appeal.

I am afraid this is going to introduce some complications. It is not going to be easy to arrange for this unless you make special references to the various courts in the different provinces. I understand that in the province of Quebec the superior court is constituted by one judge, and that is a court of appeal from inferior courts.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes.
It would not be so simple a matter as it appears at first sight.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
What I object to arc the words in the subsection which provide for an appeal to a single judge. What my amendment provides is that such an appeal shall be heard by at least two judges. If the committee thinks the amendment should not be made, I would propose that we should strike out the words :
Which orders may amongst other things provide that any such appeal may be heard and determined by a single judge.
Because there is a distinct understanding that such an appeal shall go to a single judge, and it might create mischief.

It is not an appeal properly so-called. It is a question of supervision or control by the court over the award of the arbitrators, and when that supervision is exercised by a judge of the court in the first instance, then there may be an appeal to the court of appeal afterwards. But, that is to be taken under the ordinary procedure which exists in the different provinces and I do not understand why we should seek to depart from the rule which has existed heretofore under the Railway Act. This section of the Bill is a mere reproduction of the old Railway Act. Why distinguish the word ' court' in the different provinces ? It is a court of original jurisdiction. What necessity is there for changing it.
The necessity is that I do not think any one judge should sit in appeal over these arbitrators.
The arbitrators are only enlightening the conscience of the court. When an appeal is taken they are merely expert witnesses.

Surely the lion. Minister of Justice does not contend that a man expects to go to a court. Surely it is intended that people will get their rights settled by the arbitration. They do not expect that they will have to go to a superior court.
What is the object of the section ?
The object of the section, as I understand it, is that if the arbitrators go wrong upon some principle upon which they have decided there shall be au appeal.
Exactly.

If it were limited to a matter of law I would not have so much to say about it, but a single judge could say that the arbitrators had erred on a question of fact as well as on a question of law. I do not think any single judge ought to be able to do that. I know it has been so until now. I know, as I said at the outset, that I am amending the law as it stands to-day, irrespective of the Bill which is before the committee. I do not think the law is good in its present form. I am saying when you are allowing an appeal from three arbitrators, two of whom must agree that it ought to take more than one man to set aside the decision of these two. I think the decision of these two ought not to be set aside on a question of fact without more than one judge to do it. An appeal from the county court goes to at least two judges. I have drawn the amendment in this way so as to make it consistent with the text of the section relating to inferior courts.
You could not make it to have universal application because one judge will review the verdict of the twelve men.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not like this parliament to say when we are providing a tribunal for settling these disputes between the railway and the landowner that we will allow the province of Ontario, or New Brunswick, or Nova Scotia, or Manitoba to say what tribunal shall sit in appeal over these arbitrators. This section says that you can take this appeal from these arbitrators to a single judge or to more than one judge, because, in all of the provinces there are courts of appeal with more than one judge. This says that no matter what may be the usual practice in an appeal from an inferior court in any province you may make a special rule which is not the general rule to allow an appeal to one judge alone.
That is exactly the procedure that prevails in this province. You can appeal from the arbitrators to one judge in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: That is exactly what I say. That is what I understood the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) to dispute.
Not at all.

I object to this appeal going to a single judge, and if that is the practice now, I think this parliament ought to correct it. The fact that it is so now'does not make it right. We are here to make these laws correct. The hon. minister of Railways and Canals would not listen to me if he were to suggest an amendment and I were to offer the objection that he was changing the law as it exists to-day. We would not be making provision for this railway commission if the railway law was all right. We are dealing with the Railway Act and amending it as far as we can to make it proper as far as relates to the railway commission and other matters. The hon. minister is amending this section and he has amended several other sections relative thereto. I am not going to dispute with hon. gentlemen opposite about what is the existing state of affairs because we agree on that point. We agree that in Ontario to-day this appeal goes to a single judge, and I am contending that it ought not go to a single judge.
Then why not amend the provincial procedure ?
That is where my difficulty is.
You can say that there shall be no appeal, and if you say there can be no appeal you can also say that there shall be an appeal, and you can therefore say what kind of an appeal there shall be.
How would my hon. friend amend this section so as to make it applicable to the conditions existing in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick ?

I thought that in all the provinces no appeal from an inferior court went to less than two judges ? If I am wrong in that, my amendment is not quite right. That is why I made it at least two. I know that in the court of appeal in Ontario there are five judges. That is more than two, and therefore my section would apply. I am not'wedded to the words of my amendment, but I think it should be provided in some way that one judge should not sit in review. I do not think we should indicate that it is proper that a single judge should review all the questions of fact and determine from a typewritten copy of what the evidence was in a case of original jurisdiction, better than two or it may be three arbitrators who have seen the witnesses. We expect the arbitrators to do their duty, and I do hope that there will not be many appeals,

but if there is an appeal it should be decided before more than one judge.

The more the suggestion is studied the more difficulty it presents. We have already declared that the court shall mean a county court as well as superior court, and if we give the county courts jurisdiction you could not make a proviso that there must be two judges. In Quebec, for instance, you could not go to a superior court because one judge constitutes that court, and therefore you would have to go to the highest court in the province. I do not think the jurisdiction of such a court should be invoked in such a case. If the limitation is $600 or $800, there would be few appeals. I should think that a county court judge, experienced in the consideration of evidence and the knowledge of the law, would be competent to decide if necessary that the award of the arbitrators may be set aside.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We seem to agree that if possible we should have this decision reviewed by more than one judge. Of course appeals will be limited if you increase the amount, but I am contending for $1,000. The appeals may be few, but every appeal is an important appeal. Even though my amendment be not accepted it would be better to strike out all the words after 'appeals' on the third last line, and then we have the province in each case providing the court of appeal from the inferior court, and we have these appeals from the arbitrators going to whatever court that may be in each province. Is not that safer than to provide that in each case it shall be an appeal to a single judge ?
I would prefer that, to the other suggestion you have made.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the section is amended by merely striking out those words which my motion provides for striking out, the result will be that in my province, whatever the proceeding for an appeal from an inferior court may' be, that proceeding will prevail. Perhaps that Is safer than specifying the number of judges. In drawing my amendment, I thought I was safe in saying two judges, because I thought that there could be no appeal in any province to less than two judges. I think we ought to fix what in our opinion ought to be the constitution of the court, and if there are appeals in any province to less than two judges strike out the words which indicate that the appeal may go to a single judge.

This section would be workable in the province of Nova Scotia if the Bill had not been changed to include the county court. With that change, I do not think it is workable. If we say that in the province of Nova Scotia the appeal shall lie 1444
to the Supreme Court, that will meet the difficulty.

I would suggest to the'' Minister of Justice that, with the assistance of gentlemen from the different provinces, on both sides of the House, a section might be drawn providing that in the province of Ontario the appeal should be to such-and-such, in the province of Quebec to such-and-such, and so on for the different provinces.

I think the 2nd subsection would be a great deal better if it said ' a superior court ' instead! of ' the court.'
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved that the word ' the ' before the word 1 court ' in line 44 be struck out, and the words 'a superior' be inserted in lieu thereof.

Amendment agreed to.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved that in the third subsection the following words be struck out: ' which orders may amongst other things provide that any such appeal may lie heard and determined by a single judge.'

I do not think it is wise to strike out those words. In the province of Ontario at present an appeal must be taken from the arbitrators either to a divisional court or to the court of appeal. Unless the rules of the province are changed, an appeal cannot be taken from an inferior court to a single judge.
I argued two appeals last year from arbitrations to a single judge.
I am not talking about what the hon. gentleman did last year. I am talking about what is allowed to be done under this section if it is passed.
Is the hon. gentleman proposing to allow a single judge to hear the appeal ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No, I am not, but I think that it is perfectly right that a single judge should, under certain circumstances, entertain an appeal. The expenses would he considerably less, and under the practice of the province of Ontario at present, and the provisions of this section, an appeal would only lie to the divisional court or the court of appeal of the province. Then if the courts of the province desire to make a change in the rule and send an appeal of this kind to a single judge, that would be for them to say.
I do not see any objection to a superior court judge hearing the appeal.

I may add that in the province of Ontario our courts are getting very considerably congested. Any body go-

mg to the court of appeal has to wait months for a decision. Even in the divisional court, you have to wait many months, whereas if you can go to a single judge, you will save this delay. The judges of our Ontario courts consider that it is equitable, that an appeal should be given to a single judge, and they make an order to such an effect. That would work out a larger measure of justice than by going to a court of appeal and having your award held up for a year and perhaps longer. I have a case of appeal now standing a year and a half.
I have one which has been standing for six years.
That is even worse. When a farmer is granted an award, he wants to get his money as speedily as possible, and the appeal should be to a court where speedy justice can be obtained.

What I want is sound justice and not speedy decisions which might not be sound justice. I prefer to wait six months and get a sound decision than go before a tribunal which I did not tliink the one best fitted to give a decision. The congestion mentioned by my hon. friend from Welland is being cured. They are now constituting another court in Toronto, and endeavouring to have two more judges appointed. They are proposing to make four divisions of the high court of justice, so as to relieve that congestion, and that will no doubt be accomplished if the hon. gentleman will bring his eloquence and ability to bear on the government to have more judges appointed. My object is to have the section amended so as to provide what the minister contemplates, namely, that this appeal should be as nearly as possible like an axipeal from an inferior court to a superior court. What I contend for is that we should have at least two judges to determine. If this parliament is not going to decide that there must be at least two judges, I think that the amendment of the Minister of Railways is the best remedy we can have, and this to provide that whatever the provision may be in each province for an appeal from an inferior to a superior court, that provision will apply to this appeal from the arbitrators. But, as I have suggested already to the hon. Minister of Justice, I think that we could manage to draw a section designating under little sub-heads to what court the appeal should lie in each province. It does not seem to me that hon. gentlemen are wedded to the one judge idea. In my opinion, the preponderance of evidence is that we should have more than one judge to review the decision of two arbitrators.
What is the practice in Ontario ?
At present the one judge holds the appeal, and that is why I have moved to amend
How does that work as a matter of fact ?
I have been trying to explain that it does not work out well.
It has worked perfectly satisfactorily.
I am giving evidence that it does not work out satisfactorily. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen to say that it does.
In what respect has it not worked satisfactorily 1
Because awards are set aside by one judge who views the evidence in a different light, reading it from a typewritten copy, from what the arbitrators did who heard the witnesses.
Is not that the same in every case ?

The principle is what I am contending for. Does the hon. gentleman think, as a general principle, that one judge who has not heard nor seen the witnesses is a better judge of the facts than two judges would be ?
If you had a half a dozen judges they would be under the same disability as regards the witnesses.

The hon. member perhaps has not noticed the particular appeal that is given here. This is not a case of an ordinary appeal. In the case of an ordinary appeal the judges who have not heard the evidence and observed the demeanour of the witnesses, cannot reverse the decision of the lower tribunal on a question of fact. We are providing a special appeal here, the widest appeal that can be known. We are saying in this Bill that you shall not only appeal like an ordinary man from the inferior to a superior court, but you shall be subject to have the decision in your favour reversed upon grounds upon which it cannot be reversed in an ordinary appeal. You are using language here to take away the benefit a man gets in the decision of a tribunal that saw the witnesses and heard their evidence, and more than that, you are proposing that oiip judge shall do that. I think we can_ draw a section that will get over that difficulty. If the amendment that such an appeal shall be heard and determined by at least two judges does not work out properly, we can draw a section in the interest of making these appeals satisfactory, so that justice may be done with as little'expense as possible, and a speedy decision may be accelerated. I am not in favour of so-called quick justice unless it is sound justice. I am contending that no one judge ought to

be allowed to reverse the decision of two arbitrators appointed in the careful way the Minister of Justice has arranged to appoint them by this Act. I would suggest that this section stand until we make it right, and provide that in the province of Ontario the appeal shall be to such and such a court, that in the province of Quebec it shall be to such and such a court, and so ou through all the provinces.

Don't strike out those words in the latter part of the section but let it stand as originally drafted, then the whole section will be perfectly workable. I think the appeal should be such a court of appeal for hearing these claims, as will be found most advantageous. In our own courts, if_ we struck out those lines, the appeal will' have to be heard by at least four judges, and that might not be necessary in the case of small claims. I think it would be better to leave the control of the constitution of the appeal court in the hands of the superior court.

The question I think is not well stated by the hon. gentleman from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). He wants to change the existing conditions for the province of Ontario. I do not apprehend any question will come up in that province. We have had a court operating there which has enabled these appeals to he entertained by a single judge. In all human probability this clause has been very well considered, because it would be necessary there to invoke a court consisting of more than one judge. There being such a clear difference of opinion among the legal gentlemen from Ontario, and the appeals likely to be taken under the Act being very few in number, I think we had better leave this clause as it stands and pass on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I cannot withdraw my amendment. I am not talking here idiy in what I have* been saying. Of course I will have to be hound by the majority of the committee, but I think my amendment is proper.
I have no doubt the hon. gentleman thinks so, but there is a difference of opinion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I have not heard any arguments showing that the principle that I am contending for is wrong.

I want to ask the hon. gentleman a question. Is there in the province of Ontario -under the Judicature Act they have there, such a system as we have in our province, by which a judge in a given case may appoint three arbitrators for the purpose of determining certain issues that are raised between parties ?

No. There is a rule stating distinctly that the courts will not refer cases to arbitration. But it often happens that counsel agree that a case is proper to be referred, and then a reference is made to a judge of a county court. But there is no board of arbitration in civil cases. When a case comes to trial counsel may agree that it may he referred to a county judge, or perhaps to the Master in Chancery. I persist in moving my amendment that subsection 3 of section 169 be amended by striking out all the words after the word 'appeals' in the fifth line, and inserting the following in lieu thereof: 'And such appeals shall be heard and determined by at least two judges.'
Amendment negatived.

speechtext:

House in committee on Bill (No. 139) respecting the St. Mary's River Railway Company.-Mr. Oliver.

On section 4,
Section 8 of chapter 79 of the statutes of 1900 is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor :-
The company may issue bonds, debentures or other securities to the extent of fifteen thousand dollars per mile of the railway and branches, and such bonds, debentures or other securities may be issued only in proportion to the length of railway constructed or under contract to be constructed.
What is the capitalization of this company ?

The company was organized some years ago, and the capital fixed at that time. I have not the Act of Incorporation before me, so cannot give the capitalization. This Act merely provides for extensions of the company's already existing line, and provides for a bond issue on the extension, but not for any increase in the capital stock.

This section covers the whole line, and authorizes a bond issue of $15,000 per mile. I do not say that this is additional to wliat was already authorized. I wanted to know the length of line and the capital stock, so that we might have some idea of the total capitalization. I hoped to hold this Bill up as an object lesson to the committee, because I felt that the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) would not promote any Bill authorizing a large capitalization, for I know his strong views on that subject. I hope to have an example to point to for the benefit of the hon. members who promote Bills authorizing a capitalization of $35,000 or $40,000 per mile. But the hon. member (Mr. Oliver) does not seem to have made very close inquiry into the matter.

I have here the statutes of 1900, chapter 79, of which relates to this Bill. It authorized a capital stock of $500,000 and has bonding powers of $10,000 per mile. This section changes it to $15,000 per mile.
What is the length of the line ?
That is not stated here.

I thought the hon. member for Alberta might know.
Mi-. OLIVER. I believe the length of the line already built is thirty miles. This authorizes extensions, the two main ones being thirty miles each.
That is sixty miles with a capital of $500,000 ?
Ninety miles, including the thirty miles already built. That is, of course, a rough estimate. But I have travelled the country, and I think I am about right.
I suppose my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) is satisfied that the capitalization is not excessive or likely to interfere with the proposed control of rates hereafter.
Inasmuch as this is a narrow-gauge line, and, with its branches, only ninety miles in length, I did not take the rates into as careful consideration as I would have done if it were a trunk line.

'Little drops of water, little grains of sand '-you know. If you have a number of small lines brought together, you may find that their total capitalization inflicts a burden upon the people which might have been prevented if we had looked carefully at the capital of each small concern when it was being chartered.

I am very glad indeed to find that the position I have taken meets with such approval from the leader of the opposition. With the support of the opposition for the principle I have always upheld, I should be glad to receive suggestions from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) and support any wise amendments to the Bill.
I am very glad that the opposition for once, has won the commendation of my hon. friend from Alberta.

I would say on behalf of this company that I think they are doing splendid work in the west. They have a large irrigation scheme and have done a great deal of work in that way. The object in asking for these branches is to extend the road from place to place through that territory. A great deal of the land belongs to the company, and it is being settled very fast. I am satisfied that the bonding powers are not too large for the enterprise they have undertaken. They are doing the work practically with their own capital. I think the committee can feel perfectly satisfied that it is justified in granting the powers asked for.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext:
As a matter of fact, the bonding privilege asked for is very much smaller than many of the railways whose Bills have been before us to-night, and I have no reason to think it is excessive. But I have been making a practice throughout the evening of asking what is the total capitalization, and also of making some inquiry as to the cost of the road, that I might judge whether or not it was wise to grant the powers asked for.
The difficulty with most of the charters applied for in parliament is that the bonding powers demanded are usually enough to construct the road without regard to the capital stock. That I am not inclined to regard as a very good principle. I think in that respect my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) and myself are pretty well

agreed. I was only trying to get a statement of the cost and the capitalization of this road, in order that I might hold it up as an example in contrast with some of the other Bills which have passed, and the capitalization of which seemed to be very ample.

I believe that charters have been granted where the bonding privilege was probably too large. But of companies which actually intended to do the work, to complete it and put the road in good shape, I have hardly ever known a case yet where that company was incorporated and built any amount of the road, that they have not had to come back to parliament for increased powers in this direction. However, I think the principle of keeping down to a reasonable amount the bonding privileges is a very good one. But what I wanted to say in this connection was that this road is, as my hon. friend says, a narrow gauge road ; so it is in some pieces, but the powers granted here are with the intention of making it a standard gauge road. That was explained in the committee. I understand that part of the road has already been constructed of the standard gauge, and that it will take fully this amount and more to make it a standard road.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

House in Committee on Bill (No. 154) to incorporate the Niagara, Queenston and St. Catharine's Railway Company.-Mr. German.
On section 4.

I wish to draw the attention of the House to the fact that the capital stock of this company has been cut down from $1,000,000 to $250,000. It is an expensive road to build in so far as it is to be built from St. Catharine's to Niagara, and then along the banks of the Niagara river crossing the ravines as far as Queenston, and then coming back on the third side of the triangle, as it were, to the city of St. Catharine's. The right of way is very expensive; the construction along the banks along the Niagara river is expensive and the promoters of the Bill say that in cutting the capital stock to $250,000 it will not enable them to build a first class road in first class condition. I move that the capital stock be increased to $500,000.
What does the chairman of the Railway Committee say to that ? I presume that all these arguments were submitted to the Railway Committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When the Bill was before the Railway Committee the promoters were asked as to the cost of the road and taking into consideration the capital stock at $250,000 and the bonding privileges which were given in the Bill, the Railway Committee considered they were quite sufficient. I think $250,000 capital stock is quite sufficient and 1 cannot agree with the motion made by Mr. Cowan.
Then, I suppose 1 might withdraw it.

I do not see that it makes any difference whether the capital stock is $250,000 or $500,000, because I do not suppose they intend to put a dollar of stock into the road. I understand from the Minister of Railways that railways are not built that way. I presume they intend to build the railway by the issuing of bonds, and it does not appear to me that it will be an expensive road to build. I asked the promoter of the Bill if they were going to ascend Queenston Heights and he replied, no, that he was going to keep down below in coming back to St. Catharines. In that way the cost of construction will be very

much less. I think the .judgment of the committee should be sustained.
Motion (Mr. Cowan) negatived : Yeas 9, nays 34.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
