Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Census, $35,000.

I notice that in the third volume of the census there are parallel columns showing the number of schedules in 1891 and 1901. Take the first item appearing in those schedules under the heading of ' Living Persons,' in 1891 there are twenty-five questions and in 1901 thirty-four. Will the hon. minister tell us what these questions are ?
I would require to have a copy of the schedules here to give that information in detail which' the hon. gentleman asks for.
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

speechtext: The hon. gentleman had better send and get them. It is very important that we should know.

While we are waiting for the information asked for by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy), I may explain briefly the reason for the reduction in the census vote for the ensuing year. The current year's vote was .$120,000, and, from present appearances, that will not all be used, but very .nearly. The vote for the ensuing year is $35,000. The reduction Is due to the fact that the work of compilation is drawing to a close. The end of the present fiscal

year will see it brought to a stage where, so far as can be estimated, very large reductions in the staff will be possible. It is anticipated that the vote for the ensuing year will complete absolutely the whole compilation. It is probable that the work of compilation will be finished by the month of January, although, there will be some slight work in closing up that vote. I am now able to give the information asked for day my hon. friend. I believe he desired to know what questions were asked in the census of 1901 with regard to living persons that were not asked in the census of 1891. I find in the book! the hon. gentleman himself quoted a paragraph at the bottom of the first page, showing that four questions which were asked in 1891 were not asked in 1901. There having been nine questions more in 1901 than in 1891, the absence of these four would mean that thirteen questions in all' must have been asked that were new in the census of 1901. There was an inquiry to ascertain the country or place of birth of each person, and the year of naturalization, if not a British citizen by birth, and the racial origin and nationality. There were also inquiries to ascertain the trade, occupation or profession, and the time each person was employed in the same, and the amount of his earnings in the year. Then about education and language, in 1901 there were additional questions as to the time at school in the year, and the language spoken, and whether a person spoke both English and French or only one, and his mother tongue. Those, I think, cover the whole list of extra questions.

The schedule states there were twenty-five questions in 1891. What the hon. gentleman is reading from the introduction does not explain what I was endeavouring to get. There were twenty-five questions asked in 1891 and there are thirty-four asked in 1901. I wanted to know if any of those asked in 1891 were dropped, and if not, what were the additional questions that were put in 1901 ?

There were four questions dropped which were asked in 1891; the place of birth, of father and mother, the origin if French Canadian-that question was not asked whether he was a French Canadian-third, whether he was unemployed during the week preceding the census, and fourth, whether he was an employer and the number of hands employed during the year. Now, to balance those four there was a question to ascertain the country or place of birth of each person. That was not asked in 1891.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that four questions were dropped, and a substitute for them is to give the place of birth, that is the same question as one of the four.

No, the place of birth of the father and mother is not the same question as the place of birth of the person himself. The question I am speaking of is the country or place of birth of each person other than the question of the place of birth of the father and mother. Another question asked was the year in which the person came into Canada, if he was born outside of Canada. That was not asked in 1891. The year of naturalization, if foreign born; his racial origin and nationality. Then there were inquiries to ascertain the trade, occupation or profession of the person, and the time he was employed therein, and the amount of earnings in the year. Then, under the head of education and language, there were additional questions as to the time at school in the year, if he was of school age, and the language spoken. Then there was a question whether he spoke both English and French, these being the official languages of this country. I have just had handed to me the whole list of questions in 1891, also the list of questions in 1901.
I was anxious to get the additional questions.

To do that 1 would have to read over the list of questions in each census and compare them, and work out those which were asked in the one which were not asked in the other. In 1901 the list figures up 34, and in 1891 only twenty-five. The order of questions is not quite the same in the two censuses and I would have to go over every question and compare it to give the hon. gentleman the information he asks. The general statement I gave a few minutes ago from the introduction of the census, shows practically what the hon. gentleman asks.

I am sure the hon. minister will recognize the fact that the committee ought to be in possession of the changes that I have asked for. Although it may involve some work, I am sure none will appreciate more than the hon. gentleman himself the importance of giving us that information. I suggest, as we cannot hope to get through the item conveniently to-night, the hon. gentleman should have an opportunity of getting that information. It is Friday night, there is a thin House, and this is a very important question as the hon. gentleman will see. I think it will be well to allow him an opportunity of getting that information.

I could not think of the House adjourning at the present time. This is a good opportunity of discussing this vote and putting it through. The hon. gentleman has had these schedules before him for a long time, and if he had chosen to look at them he could have compared them and made out

exactly what he wants. I could work it out myself with fifteen or twenty minutes study, hut I do not think my seat in the House of Commons is the place to do that. When 1 consider that the schedule of 1891 has been published for twelve years and that the other has been published for two years, it does not seem quite reasonable that a work of that kind should be asked for in the House of Commons by the minister who is endeavouring to pass his items. I think it is hardly fair to expect the minister on a vote of this kind, to go over the information which is patent on the face of the returns which have been published for years, and which can be obtained at any moment with a few minutes work if any body chooses to go at it.

I might be able to agree with the hon. gentleman that the hon. minister would not be expected to work out at his desk in the House of Commons such information, or in fact any other information that is asked in getting a vote like this passed, but the hon. gentleman, I am sure, will assent to the proposition that his deputies should be prepared with the work, and if they are not prepared with it the hon. gentleman has no right to ask for this vote. The hon. gentleman surely cannot ask this committee to pass these estimates involving thousands of dollars of expenditure unless we know what the value of this expenditure was. I agree that it is not the time now for the hon. minister to sit down and work out these tables, but he should be prepared through his deputies to give such information to the committee, and X appeal to the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) if it is a fair thing to ask us to go on at the close of the week with other parts of the estimates and say that we have no business to ask such questions, when there are records that we may appeal to. The hon. Minister of Finance usually gives the information that is required of him. He does not ask us to go and hunt up the information that the minister ought to have. It is the minister's business to know through his deputies and give that information to the House. I think 1 am not at all unreasonable in asking this. There has been a large increase in the cost. If the money has been well spent, the minister should have credit for it, if not the committee has a right to criticise it and it has a right to the information.

I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that we ought to be prepared to give all such information. I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me, on the other hand, that it is quite possible in committee for any hon. gentleman to ask questions that a minister cannot be ready to answer offhand, and if he gives the assurance that later on such information will be brought down, the committee should be content with that.
If any hon. gentleman wanted to do so, he could ask a series of questions that would embarrass a minister and which he could not possibly answer offhand. The only protection the minister has is to give the member the assurance that the information will be brought down in due course, but I do not think we should delay the proceeding of the House on that account. There will be ample oppoi'tunity to get this information later on, and if the hon. minister gives the assurance that it will be brought down, I think that ought to satisfy my hon. friend.

I have asked one of my officers to get that information. I think he can get it in half an hour. In the meantime the hon. gentleman can go on with other questions, so that we can proceed with the business of the House. I do not think I am asking anything unreasonable in asking the hon. gentleman to wait for half an hour for the information which he requires and which is being prepared.

The hon. minister knows very well that it is not this side that is delaying this vote. No minister can complain if questions are asked which the committee are entitled to have answered. I want to say a word to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance.- I should have to be much more reasonable than the hon. gentleman is, and I think he is a very reasonable man, if I were satisfied with the proposition he has made. The hon. gentleman surely was not hinting that the questions which are being asked this evening have the slightest embarrassing effect upon the hon. Minister of Agriculture. I should rather judge, from the intimation of the hon. gentleman, that embarrassing questions are put. They are not embarrassing unless the minister is unprepared. If the minister is unprepared all such questions are embarrassing. Large sums of money have been expended and I am sure the hon. Minister of Finance will not be so unreasonable as to press the question unless we are prepared to get all the information in detail. The hon. gentleman is a very busy man. I think he can see that members of the opposition cannot be idle men. They have very much to do. The proper stage at which we should have information, as the hon. gentleman knows perfectly well, as an old parliamentarian, is when the item is under consideration, and when the subject is fresh in our minds. To bring down that information afterwards, at a time when there is no opportunity to pay attention to it is utterly useless for a fair and intelligent criticism. I do not desire to ask unreasonable questions.

I am afraid the hon. gentleman has used the word ' embarrassing ' in a sense different from what I have used it. These questions are not embarrassing except as questions

to be answered at tlie moment. These questions will be answered within a reasonable time. They are only embarrassing in the sense that my hon. friend insists upon the hon. Minister of Agriculture answering them at a particular moment. If he gets the assurance that the information will be furnished I do not imagine that he would wish the business of the House delayed while we get it.

It is an unfair thing to ask the opposition not to press for an answer when the vote is under consideration. The hon. minister should be ready with his answers right now, and it is not the fault of the opposition that he is not ready. [DOT]
1 have informed my hon. friend that I will have the answer within half an hour, and it may be within a few minutes.
' Deaths in public institutions.' Thirteen questions were asked in 1S91 and thirty-five were asked in 1901.

My hon. friend has not read it quite correctly. In 1891 ' deaths in ^niblic institutions ' comes second and not first, but in 1901 it comes third. The difference in the figures is the difference between thirteen and fifteen.

I am very sorry that the minister has chosen this time to bring up this estimate when there is a very thin House. The hon. gentleman is not responsible for that, but he does take responsibility if he presses the matter to a vote unless we have the information. Why should not the minister come down to the House at the next sitting prepared with answers to such questions as may be asked regarding the meaning of the schedules. I am sure the hon. gentleman will save time if he does that.

I regret that the hon. gentleman did not move for a return because it will involve an elaborate calculation and take considerable time. If the hon. gentleman thinks for a moment that we wish to burk inquiry or refuse information, I shall be very glad to leave this vote and take other votes in my department, and I ask the hon. gentleman's assistance to pass these votes tonight so that the House will make reasonable progress. We can take the item for exhibitions.
Exhibitions, $150,000.

The vote for the current year of $195,000 has not been all expended. It was expected that the Louisiana Purchase Exhibition at St. Louis would open in May of this year. It has been postponed until 1904. The vote included also the exhibition at Osaka, Japan, which opened on the 1st of March last and will close on the 1st of August.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Osaka exhibition has been provided for out of the current year's vote except a comparatively small amount which will have to be expended between the 1st ot Juiy and the 1st of August. The St. Louis exhibition is to be held in the ensuing year, and I am asking $150,000 to have Canada properly represented there. The exhibition will open on the 1st of May next and will continue until the 1st of December, so that next year I will have to ask for a portion of the expenditure. The vote taken now will prepare the exhibits and the accommodation necessary and enable us to carry on the work until the 1st bf July, 1904. It is represented that the St. Louis exhibition will be a magnificent one. There is always a rivalry between Chicago and St. Louis and (lie St. Louis people are endeavouring to eclipse the great Columbia exhibition at Chicago in 1904. The people of the state, the citizens of St. Louis, the national government, and a number of the states have combined to contribute large sums of money, one circular representing that $30,000,000 would be spent by the people of the United States on the exhibition. Under these circumstances I feel that it is very important indeed that Canada shall make a creditable exhibition there because I believe it will help to make-or rather to sustain, because it is already made-the reputation of our country as a place of glorious production, immense capabilities, and splendid possibilities.
What will be the total cost ?

We have spent about $0,000 out of the current year's vote on preparations. I hope the .$150,000 will carry on the work during the ensuing year, although I cannot be positive of that until next spring when the exhibition opens. If I find it to be necessary I would be disposed to ask for a supplementary vote. We hope now that the $150,000 will carry us to the 1st of July, 1904. with the probability of spending $60.000 in the following fiscal year ; say $225,000 altogether in round figures.
Are we erecting buildings.

The exhibition provides the buildings. The arrangement is that the exhibits shall be classified according to their character and they refuse to allow any national exhibition in any one building. In explanation of that I may say that at Glasgow, at Wolverhampton. at Cork, and at Osaka, we concentrated the exhibits in one building, and in that way made a more effective display, and one more economically and efficiently managed. I think it is a much more effective way of displaying our resources, and directing attention to our country. But in St. Louis, the plan and scope of the exposition will not admit of that. We have to put our

agricultural exhibits in the agricultural building, our horticultural exhibits in the horticultural building and so on through all the classes. But it is proposed to have a Canadian building there, which will contain offices for our commissioner and staff, and which will be a rallying point for Canadian visitors and for persons desiring to obtain information about Canada. That would probably involve the erection of a moderate sized Canadian building.

I suppose the hon. gentleman will be able to give to the committee some idea as to how this sum of money, which he is asking for, is to be spent-how much in buildings, how much in exhibits, aud so on.

We have not yet had plans submitted for the building, but it will probably cost $20,000 or $25,000. The space for our exhibits in the large buildings is given free, and the ground for our own building is also given ifree by the authorities. As our exhibits will be scattered in a large number of buildings, we shall be obliged to have a large staff to watch over them and keep them in order and explain them to visitors. If we had them all in one building, we would not require more than one-third or perhaps one-fourth of the staff that will be required. There will be considerable expense incurred in collecting the exhibits. We have found it desirable that the government should collect and manage exhibits of natural products-agricultural, horticultural, mineral, and forest exhibits-as we cannot get individual exhibitors in these lines to work up creditable exhibits. That has been our course at all the great expositions. [DOT] That work requires a considerable amount of preparation and a considerable expenditure of money. One part of that exhibit, in which we have been uniformly very successful, is a cold storage establishment, in which our products are displayed behind glass throughout the whole exhibition. That is an expensive exhibit, but it is a very striking and attractive one, and has always attracted an immense amount of attention. Then there will be the maintenance of the staff, the carriage of the exhibits to the exposition and return, and the incidental expenses. The estimate which is here made has been made upon our experience of other exhibitions.
Can the hon. gentleman give us approximately the cost of the cold storage plant, the salaries of those employed, and the cost of transportation ?

When we were fixing the amount of this vote, I discussed with the exhibition commissioner the amount that would probably be required, and he made a set of figures which were quite approximate, as my hon. friend will understand. I have not them at the moment in my mind ; but, speaking
from memory, the cold storage plant, including installation, carrying on and management, will probably cost $5,000 or $6,000. Salaries and wages fer the whole year, roughly speaking, will come to $20,000 or $25,000, that is for the Canadian staff, in addition to which we always have to employ temporary labour from day to day ns we need it. The collection of exhibits in the four classes that I have spoken of would come to at least $50,000 or $00,000, which, I think, is an inside figure for all the work of searching, collecting and preparing them. I have been requested by some of those interested in Canada to make a live stock exhibit at St. Louis. If that should be undertaken, it would involve an expenditure of $250,000.
Does the hon. gentleman propose to make a live stock exhibit at the expense of the country ?

I have not answered the request. But even supposing the country would not pay the expenses of the individual exhibitors, if Canada does make a live stock exhibit, the management of that will cost the department probably $50,000. I have not yet decided on that, as there is an objection to a live stock exhibit in St. Louis, owing to the fact that it is extremely hot there in summer and many of our best breeders would not like to send their best atiimalg to St. Louis in that season. If we cannot get their best animals, it would be useless to have an exhibit of live stock there at all.
In the $60,000 required to defray the expenses of placing an exhibit in St. Louis, is any expenditure on live stock included ?

Not in that item. That is just the item of the four classes-agricultural, horticultural, forestry and mineral exhibits. These have to be collected from all parts of the country. To-day the farmers are growing grain for us by special arrangement to be sent to the exhibit at St. Louis. We are making every effort to make our display an impressive one. In days gone by we have been very successful at the different exhibitions, and as this exhibition is still more important than those which preceded it, we must do everything possible to give our country a very effective showing.
How will the building compare with the one we had at the Pan-American ?

It will 'be much finer. The building at the Pan-American cost us $14,000 or $15,000. . We expect to spend on this $25,000, and perhaps more, as the cost of building will be much heavier. The labour people in St. Louis are making arrangements to charge very high rates.

It is to be hoped that we will have a much better buildiug than the one we had at the Pan-American. From the expression I have heard from a number of Canadian visitors, that buildiug was totally unworthy of this great country. Even if we should have to spend two or three times ithe amount we should not hesitate to do it in order to have a proper building. Has the site been selected ?

Yes, a very favourable site has been allotted to us, not far from the exhibition office and close to the agricultural exhibition building. Our exhibition commissioner went all over the ground and located the site in conjunction with the president of the exhibition association there.

That is an import-amt item. The site of the buildiug at the Pan-American was very detrimental to the appearance of the building itself and it is to be hoped that a better location will be found at St. Louis.

At the Pan-American the site was very much injured by a large restaurant being built just opposite, and another inferior building just along side, but that was not understood when we secured our site.

I do not think that there will be any disposition on this side to oppose any reasonable vote that will enable Canada to take at this exhibition the proud place she has taken at other exhibitions. I think it would be a great mistake to count too closely the cost. I join with my hon. friend from South Grey in pointing out that there was a general expression of, disappointment on the part of Canadian visitors to the Pan-American, both at the location and the character of our building. As regards the location, the government made the reasonable excuse that they had to take whatever they could get, but I am glad to hear that we are to be better treated at the St Louis exhibition. While dealing with the question of the Pan-American, perhaps the hon. gentleman will tell the committee what was the winding up of that exhibition, and what disposition was made of the buildings and the large outfit we had there ?

The hon. gentleman has spoken of the furniture. That did not belong to us, but was an exhibit made and loaned by the Canada Furniture Company, a combination, I might call it, of the furniture manufacturers with headquarters in Toronto. They wished to show their furniture, and loaned it to us in the understanding that it was to be used in the Canadian building.' So we spent nothing on it, except some .$200 at the end of the exhibition to make good some little damage. The building was, I Hon. Mr. FISHER.
might say, simply got rid of. At the end of the Buffalo exposition we had almost to beg people to take the building off the grounds, as was required of us under the contract we made with the exhibition people. We sold the glass and some other parts of the building for $622.50, and the building itself for about $200 or $250. The contractor had to take it down and remove it. In the case of many of the other buildings, those who had built them were called upon to pay large sums to have them taken away and so fulfil their bargain with the exhibition authorities, which was similar to ours. My hon. friend can understand that, with so many buildings thrown on the market at the end of such an exhibition it would be practically impossible to get anything for them. At the Wolverhampton and Glasgow exhibitions our buildings were put up by contractors under agreement that the contractors should take them back at the close of the exhibition. So we got the buildings for the purpose for which we needed them for a less price. But we could not make such a contract in Buffalo, although, I am satisfied that the system is a good one.

I notice among the items of expenditure in connection with these exhibitions that many purchases have been made in the country where the exhibitions have taken place. Would it not be better to buy Canadian furniture and fittings throughout, so as to have everything as far as possible of Canadian manufacture V This would help our producers and would be likely to attract more attention at the exhibition. Would it not be worth while also for the hon. minister to consider if we could not make an arrangement for the designing of a building in Canada and the preparation of the material here ? For instance, the roofing material, whether tin or galvanized iron, could be manufactured in Canada as we have large producers in that line. Of course, the lumber could be Canadian. Then, the carpeting, fittings and furniture could be supplied here. The arrangement of the hon. gentleman made with the Canadian Furniture Company for the supply of furniture at the Pan-American was, I think, a splendid arrangement. It filled every purpose from a Canadian standpoint. I would like information with regard to one particular item of expenditure for the Pan-American. There is an item here-the W. C. Edwards Company, two oak stands for grain exhibits, $745. This seems a very large item for such a purpose. What has become of the stands referred to ?

Let me answer the hon. gentleman's last question first. The stands lie refers to are at the experimental farm waiting for the St. Louis exhibition. They are large erections, and the two stood in the main hall

at Buffalo. They are of hardwood, polished, and elaborate in their construction.
Were they made under contract ?
A bargain was made before they were ordered.
Does the hon. minister regard that as a good plan for-

Yes, I think so. I may explain that 1 have been very fortunate in having the services of a gentleman who has been most successful in the decorative work of our agricultural exhibitions. I refer to Mr. Hay, who used to be accountant at the experimental farm, but whom I may now call a permanent officer of our exhibition staff. For live years, ever since the Paris exhibition, he has been engaged in decorative work in connection with the agricultural displays we have made at the various exhibitions. He has made a most wonderful success of this work. Our agricultural decorations at these exhibitions attract great attention and win universal admiration, and have been the means of our gaining a great deal of credit. I may say that Mr. Hay designed the Canadian arch in London on the occasion of the King's coronation, and succeeded in making a display of grain and other agricultural products which attracted the favourable attention of the millions present. The stands referred to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) were designed by Mr. Hay for the express purpose for which they were used. The hon. gentleman spoke of Canadian materials in our buildings. These buildings are made of rough lumber covered with staff or stucco, and must be made on the spot. The wood being entirely covered, there is no particular object to be served in having it taken from Canada, particularly as the expense of taking Canadian material to cities where the exhibitions are held would be very heavy. If we were to follow that course, we should also have! considerable difficulty with the contractors. We have found it best to put up these buildings by contract, and the contractors themselves wish to furnish the materials, as they find it most convenient for themselves. Even at Buffalo, so near Canada, we found it impossible to supply the material ourselves. For instance, we have in Canada firms that supply a very fine metallic roofing, which has been widely exhibited. But that concern would not undertake to supply the roofing for our building in Buffalo for anything like what we could get it done for there. I believe their price was something like four or five times what the contractors put the roof on for. The roofing concern wished to exhibit, but they did not want to roof our building, and to have got them to do it would have greatly increased the cost. I grant that the hon. gentleman's idea is a taking one, and it is
one which possesed my mind on the occasion of the Buffalo exhibition. But it was not found feasible.

On the question of the two oak stands supplied by W. C. Edwards & Company for $745, I do not think that the hon. gentleman's explanation will be wholly satisfactory to the committee. The objection I raised is this, that you spend $745 for stands to put grain upon, and you take them around to the different exhibitions, first at the Pan-American and now at St. Louis, and the people who go to these exhibitions see just the same thing.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE That is only a part of the exhibit.

It is a very important one. Here is an appropriation of $745 for stands to put grain upon. I say that no matter what decorator yon have, you send him to the Pan-American exhibition and he puts grain upon these stands, they are decorated in one way. The minister says they are now in Ottawa waiting to be sent to St. Louis. Now, the exhibition in St. Louis must be very similar to the Pan-American. I look upon that expenditure as too large altogether. It would be better to make such changes as advancement would require. The hon. gentleman's idea is quite correct. Those stands are made so that they may be adapted to circumstances. In connection with the matter of a live stock exhibit I would like to know what association representing live stock breeders asked the hon. minister for the amount that he says they have asked him for.
All live stock associations in Ontario had a joint meeting not long ago at which they passed a resolution, and I am informed that in other provinces they have done the same.
Whence comes the protest that the stock would likely be injured by the heat at St. Louis ?

There was no protest from an association, but a number of breeders themselves told me that while they had no objection to an exhibit being made they did not think they would like to send their best animals to the exhibition at St. Louis during the heated term.
It was only some individual breeders who said that ?
Yes.
You have no protest from the association that asked for the money ?
None.
You are influenced by individuals as against the request of the association.

I said that the question was an open one and that I had not decided. I did not say that it had been settled. I simply stated the diffi-

culties there were in connection with the live stock exhibit.

I can see no objection at all in the fact that one or two men do not see fit to send their animals to such an exhibition as the St. Louis exhibition is to be. Because a few men are not disposed to do that why should the whole exhibition be stopped ? I think the Breeders' Association which has asked for this grant will require some more lucid explanation than has been given in that respect.
Explanation as to what ?
An explanation as to the reason why the minister would not give an answer to this association ?

I did not say that that was the reason why I did not give an answer. I said I was discussing and considering the question, and I shall be prepared to give an answer. I pointed out that certain people had said that they did not care to send their best animals to St. Louis during the hot weather and that weighed with me to a certain extent.
May I ask the hon. minister when a decision will be arrived at ?
Before long, I hope.
Is there any exhibit that can be taken to St. Louis that will bring greater profit to this country than an exhibit of live stock ?
I think, if a successful exhibit can be made there, it will be most advantageous to the country.

I would like to ask the hon.
minister if there is any strong intimation given by the breeders by way of protest, implied or otherwise, or in the way of suggestion of the difficulties of taking valuable stock there, and if that objection were adhered to by the breeders in Canada it would go so far as to affect the character of the exhibit, or to interfere with our placing the best stock that can be produced in Canada on exhibition. If it had that effect I think it would be a great mistake for Canada not to have the best stock there and that we should either have the best or none.
Quite so.

My hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) has pointed out to-night that it would be a serious thing if our Canadian breeders should draw the line too closely. People would be wanting in loyalty so to speak, in presenting the case of Canada not to assist the hon. minister in every way, even at some slight risk, and an exhi-145
bition from Canada devoid of that branch would, I think, be very much impaired. But, on the other hand, if there is a possibility of not making the show that Canada could make there, it would be equally as great a mistake. I must admit the gravity of the question and I hope the hon. minister will succeed, as my hon. friend from Macdonald suggests, in inducing the Canadian breeders to assist him in carrying out what no doubt is the wish of Canadians generally.
I would like to ask the hon. minister how the selection of live stock was made in connection with other exhibitions, for instance, the Pan-American exhibition.

By the Live Stock Association. There was a dairy contest at Buffalo and in connection with that work of selecting and obtaining the cows to go into it it was left in the hands of the live stock commissioner of my department. He worked in co-operation with the Live Stock Association but he did most of the work of selecting the animals.
If the hon. minister decides to have a live stock exhibit at St. Louis, will the same policy be pursued ?
I should say so. It was successful before and I think it ought to be carried out again.
Is the hon. gentleman seeking to procure any information as to the months in which the live stock is to be exhibited ?

The authorities of the exhibition have been asked over and over again to give ns information in regard to that, but we have not been able to obtain it. I do not think they have yet formulated their own plans. In consequence of the representations that were made to me by the Live Stock Association, I am arranging for a delegation to come down and discuss that question.
I suppose the hon. minister recognizes the importance of such an exhibit in that particular portion of the United States ?
Certainly.

I suppose he understands the enormous amount of high grade cattle that have been taken into Missouri, Kansas and Illinois. I cannot understand why the hon. minister should for a moment entertain the proposition of any individual breeders as against the proposition of the association which represents all the high class breeders in the country. I trust the hon. gentleman is seeking information as to the months during which the live stock exhibit will be held, and also as to what the mortality would likely be or has been in that state of Missouri during the months when the fair is likely to be held.

The mortality in the state would be no indication of the work of an exhibition. It is well understood how severe exhibition work is on the animals exhibited, because, during an exhibition, the difficulties in a hot place like St. Louis would be very much accentuated. If these breeders will pledge themselves to send their stock, nobody will be more pleased than myself to make an exhibit that will be creditable to Canada, but, as the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) says, if we find a considerable number of live stock breeders who say that they cannot afford to send their best animals it would be a misfortune to be represented by second rate animals.
Who are the breeders who have made these representations ?
I cannot give the names at this moment.

I think we should have that information later on so that the Breeders' Association which has made the request for a grant may know. The least the hon. minister owes to this association is that he should let them.know who the men are who are objecting.

I have not said any men are objecting. I have said that they have represented to me the danger and difficulty of sending stock to St. Louis during the hot weather and I doubt whether they would be willing to send their best animals. I am not setting that against the representations of the association. but merely putting it forward as one of the difficulties in connection with the live stock exhibit which I conceive it my duty to consider.
The minister left the impression on my mind that it was his intention to do it.
That is entirely a wrong impression, because I stated positively that the matter was under consideration.
The association should know from what source these protests come.

If the minister is not in a position to tell the House during what particular months the live stock will be exhibited there, I do not see how individual breeders could object when they do not know themselves. I agree with the minister that if it was the general opinion among the breeders not to send their first class animals there, it would be much better that we should have no exhibition at all. If this objection emanated from some gentlemen who are not yet aware as to what particular months they are expected to send their animals there, it can only have come from q few of them at the most. Can the minister tell us what pro-Mr. BOYD.
portion of the breeders have objected ? Every consideration should be given by the minister to the representations of the Breeders' Association both in the east and in the west.

Mr. Hutchison is the commissioner and Mr. Brodie is the acting secretary. Mr. Burns is acting secretary at Osaka.
At the Glasgow Fair there was more than one commissioner.

There has been no discussion on that point yet.
Is Colonel O'Brien connected in any way with this exhibition ?
No.
I might put in a word on behalf of Colonel O'Brien. He is a faithful follower of the government, and I think it would be acceptable to him if he were to get employment ?
He is a very good man.
It would only be fair return for the political services he reuders to the government.
That is not the way we do this work.
I see some very familiar names here. A. N. C. Treadgold got $491 for interest and expenses on gold exhibits at the Glasgow exhibition.
Mr. Treadgold had a collection of Klondike nuggets and he offered it to ns and we undertook to pay the interest on the value and the insurance.
Who is Mr. Treadgold V

The selection was made on the authority and advice of Colonel Gourdeau, deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

Among other familiar names we have McPherson and Schell of Alexandria, who got paid for cheese boxes. Is that Mr. Schell the member for Glengarry ?
I cannot tell whether he is or not.
Perhaps some of the minister's officials could tell him.
I cannot say just who the gentleman is. He is Mr. Schell, of Alexandria. Whether he is the member of parliament for Glengarry or not, I do not know.
Will the minister tell us at the next meeting of the committee ?
I will try to do so.

In case he proves to be tlie member for Glengarry, may I ask whether members of parliament will be preferred in future for supplies ?
