I see that for decorating and dressing exhibits Cl. Damond was paid $803. Is that the gentleman who the hon. minister said had charge of the decorations in connection with the different exhibitions ?
No, Mr. Hay was the man I mentioned. I should imagine that is for the supply of materials, but I do not know.
Is the minister able to say what form that gold exhibit took 1' Was it in the shape of nuggets ?
It was almost altogether nuggets, but there was a little dust also.
Did these nuggets come from the Yukon or British Columbia ?
Those I refer to came from the Yukon. There were others that came from British Columbia, which were supplied by the provincial authorities.
What other exhibits had you from British Columbia ?
We had a large mineral exhibit, given, I believe, by the provincial Department of Mines. We had also forestry and wood products, grains, foods and fish from British Columbia.
I suppose it is not usual to pay interest on gold-dust and nuggets. The gentleman would scarcely expect to deposit them and get interest on them from the banks.
Oh, yes, gold-dust may be turned into money at any time. We asked to have the use of them just as we might ask to have the use of so many dollars and pay interest on them.
Had Mr. Treadgold any interest in that exhibit other than that, as I suppose, he had a concession that he was advertising at the time ?
I am not aware of it. Mr. Treadgold owned the nuggets and loaned them to us, and we paid him for the loan of them.
Had he a concession in the Yukon at that time ?
I do not know. I had nothing to do with the concessions.
Was he the same man who had the concession ?
I believe he is. I know him personally, aud I always took for granted that he was the man who got the concessions.
He was at that time, I suppose, attempting to float some scheme ?

I do not know the dates of Mr. Tread-gold's various Investments or schemes. But bis name never appeared on those nuggets. Nobody who saw them knew that they came from him, or knew where they came* from beyond the fact that they were from the Yukon. All that appears on them were the names of the creeks or mines from which they came.
Who owned the mines from which they came ?

I cannot tel! the hon. gentleman that. I haven't them in my mind, and I do not know that we have a list of them ; but they were all in the Yukon. I may add that the transaction was arranged through the high commissioner's office in London.
It does not change Mr. Treadgold's interest in the transaction whether it was arranged in the high commissioner's office or in the hon. gentleman's.
No, but the fact that bis name did not appear on the exhibits would dispose of the idea that they were used by him for advertising purposes.
Perhaps the hon. minister can recall what mines were mentioned and who was associated with the mines ?

I am informed that there was no name of any individual claim or mine. There was simply the name of the creek, such as Bonanza or Eldorado, over the specimens which came from that creek ; but the individual claim or mine or washing from which they came was not put on.
Does the hon. gentleman say that they bore the name of any creeks or localities that are in any way associated with the Treadgold concession ?

I confess I do not know .lust now what those creeks are, and I cannot tell exactly what creek the specimens came from, and consequently I cannot tell whether the names of those particular creeks were over the exhibits or not. But I believe that some of the richest claims were on the creeks whose names were mentioned.
Did the department or the high commissioner decide to make the exhibit of the gold nuggets, or did this whole matter originate with the High Commissioner in England ?

I cannot say exactly where it originated. We were discussing our mining exhibit, and the question arose where we could get at reasonable cost some gold exhibits. Speaking entirely from memory, it seems io

me that I received a letter from the High Commissioner stating that this exhibit was in London, and that we could get it on reasonable terms, and that I replied asking the High Commissioner to arrange to get it.

The fact is that Mr. Tread-gold had these exhibits in the old country, and was advertising them in the interests of his mining speculations, and I suppose he suggested to somebody representing the Canadian government that it would be a good idea to have those nuggets exhibited at the expense of the government.
When the arrangement was made this gold was in transit from the Yukon to London, and was not in London. It arrived after the arrangement was made.

When the nuggets were in transit an arrangement was entered into by the High Commissioner to pay Mr. Tread-gold $491 for the use of them as an exhibit. Will the hon. minister regard that as a proper way to make a collection of the gold of the Yukon ? Would it not have been better for him to have made the collection on his own behalf ? Evidently Mr. Treadgold made a selection of the nuggets to advertise his concession, the government paid him $491 for the use of that collection as an exhibit, and Mr. Treadgold got all the advantage of the advertisement without any expenses, and made a profit on it beside.

As a matter of fact, this collection was not made for the purposes of the exhibition. But the government seized the opportunity of getting hold of a good collection of nuggets from the Yukon, and was fortunate in having had the opportunity. The arrangement was made to pay five per cent interest on the value of the gold and the insurance, and it seems to me that the government is to be congratulated for having been able to get a good collection of nuggets at that low price. To have made a similar collection ourselves would have entailed a good deal of expense. There was no advertisement of Mr. Treadgold's nuggets.
Could the hon. gentleman not have borrowed the money on the credit of Canada at as low a rate ?
Yes.

Then there can be no question of the saving of interest in that case. Does it not occur to the hon. gentleman that the government was made use of by Mr. Treadgold for the purpose of advertising his mining scheme ? The excuse offered by the hon. gentleman, namely, that these nuggets were accepted because Canada would have had to invest a good deal of money and lose the interest on it in making a collection of its own, is the last reason that

should be offered in a case of that kind. Has the hon. the Finance Minister brought the treasury into discredit by permitting such a transaction ? He is fond of boasting about his surplus of millions, and yet we have to capture an individual on the road and get him to part with his nuggets for the purposes of exhibition. The government accepted Mr. Treadgold's nuggets and paid him the interest ; that was not done in the interest of Canada, but for the special advantage of Mr. Treadgold and his scheme.

1 suppose it is because I am not blessed with such a lively imagination as my hon. friend, that I cannot see the evil in the transactions that he does. I cannot see any criticism he has made on it which would not apply to the obtaining of gold from any other living being. The government does not keep a stock of nuggets on hand. It will be generally admitted that the resources of Canada should be represented at these exhibitions. If we are making an exhibit of minerals, would it not be desirable that we should have an exhibit of gold from the Yukon and British Columbia and Nova Scotia ; and if we are to have such an exhibit, how are you going to get the gold ? The government do not keep it in stock. They must buy it or rent it, and wherever they get the gold they have to take the representation of those who own it as to the part of Canada from which it is taken ; and if on this particular exhibit the name of that portion of Canada from which it came was placed on it, where was the wrong ? The hon. member insisted that the name of Mr. Treadgold wa| on it.
I did not, from first to last, say or insist that his name was on it.
The hon. gentleman said it was used to advertise Mr. Treadgold's concession, but how could that be done if his concession was not mentioned in connection with it ?
I will tell the hon. gentleman later on.

It seems to me utterly impossible. If gold nuggets are accepted and they come from British Columbia, or the Yukon, or from some particular creek in Canada, is there anything wrong in our saying so ? In all our mineral exhibits, the place where each exhibit comes from is always indicated. We have dealt with this as we would have dealt with any other mineral exhibit. We placed it as a specimen of the wealth of Canada, and put on it a label telling what portion of Canada it came from. As to paying the interest, if we bought gold sovereigns we would have to pay the interest. And I think that when the Minister of Agriculture was able to make an arrangement for which he got the gold at simple interest at five per cent, that
was a reasonable and fair and honourable arrangement ; and any person, including my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), if he were serious, would congratulate the Minister of Agriculture upon making such an excellent arrangement for exhibiting the gold of Canada.

I am quite ready to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture upon the simplicity which led to his being imposed upon. I do not attribute anything wrong to the minister. He has stated, what is, no doubt, the fact, that the arrangement was made not through him but through the High Commissioner.
He says it is a good arrangement.

Then, come to the other part of it. I stated that Mr. Treadgold's concession was advertised through the machinery and at the expense of Canada. His specimens were accepted and he was paid interest on them. When this is objected to, the answer was given that specimens had to be had somewhere. But let us see whether Mr. Treadgold or Canada was advertised. Mr. Treadgold was, naturally, anxious to bring his concessions to the notice of the investing public-these concessions that he had bought-no, I should almost apologize for saying that he bought them-the concessions that were given to him. Mr. Treadgold himself fixed the places where these specimens came from- there was no other way. Of course, every one of them would be announced as coming from some spot within the limits of his concession, and the.effect of the arrangement was to advertise the specimens from Mr. Treadgold's concession at the expense of the country. So, I do not retract one word that I said, that Canada paid a sum-not enough to bankrupt the country, being only $400-for the use of specimens which were exhibited at our expense for his benefit. I think it would have been better had he paid Canada some thing to take charge of his exhibit. Of course, Mr. Treadgold did not take specimens to England to advertise other people's claims, but to advertise his own, and every one would be marked as coming from his concessions. I am not sure that no one can see more clearly than the Minister of Finance that Canada not only advertised Mr. Treadgold's concessions, but, in the form of interest on his specimens, paid him for the privilege of doing so.

As I view the matter, there is not the slightest foundation for the statements the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) is making. Every word he has said against the marking of these specimens with the locality of their origin would apply equally to a piece of stone, a column of coal, or a specimen of silver-lead ore. The origin of these things had to be marked upon them. When I go

through the Imperial Institute in London, I see specimens of Canada's mineral wealth, all marked, showing the portion of Canada from which they come. No doubt, Mr. Treadgold's specimens were treated as the other specimens were. Mr. Treadgold was the only person who could tell where they came from. Those who furnished specimens, being responsible people, would be looked to for that information and their statements would be accepted. If these specimens were labelled as coming from Eldorado creek or Bonanza, that would be following precisely the same course as would be followed in the case of a piece of silver-lead ore marked as coming from Rossland. I have no knowledge of the case except what has been stated here to-night, but I understand that these specimens were not labelled with Mr. Treadgold's name or with anything to associate them with his concession.
Is the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) prepared to say that these specimens were not associated, in the way of being labelled with the locality of origin, with Mr. Treadgold's concession ?

I have already said that I have no knowledge of the case except what has been furnished by this discussion, and I presume that most members of the committee are in the same position. I say that, according to the information furnished by the Minister of Agriculture, these were not associated with Mr. Treadgold's concession or Sir. Treadgold's business venture, but they were marked with the place of origin, just as any other mineral specimens were. It would be as reasonable to say that because a specimen of ore was marked as coming from Rossland, B.C., you were trying to promote the interest of some speculator in Rossland. The whole thing is utterly absurd.

It is quite usual for people from the province of Ontario and elsewhere to exhibit as private persons or companies. We found such exhibits at the Pan-American, and they are to be found at every exhibition. It is perfectly right to use such exhibits for the promotion of business interests of the exhibitor. But does anybody suppose that Sir. Tread-gold having these concessions, that he was endeavouring to place upon the English market, would give as the place of origin i of any of these specimens any claim that was not covered by his own concessions ? Sly hon. friend may be imposed upon in some other way, but I am sure that he sees how Canada was imposed upon in this case.
I wish to point out the difference between specimens of gold and specimens of coal or any other mineral. Though Sir. Tread-gold was probably in the way of making his own exhibit, the government received Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
his specimens, marked, no doubt, as coming from claims in Sir. Treadgold's concession, and allowed him interest upon them. The expense involved was a small sum, but to that extent, Canada was used entirely for Mr. Treadgold's purposes.

I will admit, for the sake of the argument, that every specimen furnished by Sir. Treadgold was marked as coming from some mine in Sir. Treadgold's concession. But that makes no difference whatever. They were treated in exactly the same way as other mineral specimens, so far as that was concerned. The only difference between specimens of gold and specimens of other minerals is that gold is an article of value, and, while you have it, you must pay interest on it, whereas the owners of coal or other less expensive products are ready to offer specimens without charge.
Yes, but the hon. gentleman was advertising Mr. Treadgold's concession as against the concessions of other people.

Then, if a specimen furnished by some British Columbia mine owner, say Mr. Dunsmuir, or some other, were marked as coming from the place of origin would that be advertising the owner's business at the expense of Canada ? The only difference, as I say, is that gold is a valuable article, and represents so many gold sovereigns, and, you can only get it by paying interest.
Has any statement been made as to what has been paid to my fellow townsman (Mr. Egan) for his exhibit ?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) was not in the House when I explained that.
The cases of birds were damaged.
But surely Mr. Egan must have been paid interest, because his specimens were articles of value.
But not valuable articles in the same class as gold.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) to claim that the amount paid was not enough ?
No, I dare say that was all right. What was the value of Mr. Egan's exhibit ?
It was sent to Paris, and, though somewhat damaged there, it was furbished up and sent on to Glasgow, but was so damaged that it was not fit to be used again.

There is one consolation in this matter, and that is that if Mr. Tread-

gold's scheme was advertised at the expense of the Dominion, it did not cost as much as another famous exploitation of the Yukon. It will be in the recollection of hon. gentlemen that when the famous Mackenzie & Mann exploitation of the Yukon was launched on the British public, it was advertised at the expense of this country, for Mr. Ogilvie went over there and lectured throughout Great Britain while under the pay of Canada in order to capture the public there.

Mr. Ogilvie was an official of the people of Canada long before this government came into jmwer, and was generally regarded as a most honourable and capable officer, and I do not think he would engage in anything which was inconsistent with his duty. I cannot contradict my hon. friend's statement, because he may have facts which 1 do not possess, but I do not think Mr. Ogilvie would take such a step at variance with his duties.

This exhibit was not the only gold exhibit, as a matter of fact there were other gold exhibits there, treated in the same way. The Bank of Commerce had a large exhibit at Glasgow and also at Wolverhampton. There were a number of other persons treated in the same way as Mr. Treadgold, and had just the same advertisement. But there was no advertisement in any shape or way. The whole mineral exhibit, wltether gold! or otherwise, is labelled showing the places from which it comes. We get the ibest specimens we can collect to show the minerals of Canada, and we label the places from which they come, just as these gold exhibits were labelled. That is the only advertisement there was, and it cannot be called one.
Would this particular exhibit of Mr. Treadgold have been exhibited! had it not been taken over by the government ?
No. It was on its way over to be sold in London, and the moment the exhibition was over it was taken by Mr. Treadgold and melted down and sold.

The most, important item the minister is asking for now is to pay for the exhibit that is to be taken to St. Louis, and the most important part of that is the live stock. Therefore I think the minister should be prepared to give the names of these individuals who object to taking live stock, which the minister says has not yet been decided on.
That is not the reason it has not yet been decided.

I think until it is decided upon, the committee should rise and this
item should not pass. At any rate, I must appeal to the Mipister of Finance and protest against the way he is forcing us to go on when so many members of the House are absent. I appeal to him, because he comes from one of the outlying districts whose members are compelled to remain here and do business, while those living nearer go away every Friday night. We find that every Friday night this HBuse is practically without representatives from the province of Quebec, and largely from Ontario. There are only two men from the province of Quebec in this Chamber tonight, and every Friday night from four o'clock onwards there is scarcely a quorum of members here. Indeed there would not be a quorum if it depended on members sitting opposite. Every Friday night these important questions are brought forward, and it is only members from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories and British Columbia who remain here. If we could get away as easily as those other men do, there would not be a quorum in the House. I protested earlier in the session at the late date at which this session was called together. Here we are now well on into June, and I am told we are to be pressed into three sessions a day in the course of another week, that we are to have ten o'clock sessions. The chief business of the session has not yet been taken up. It is well known that the most important issues that were to engage the attention of this House were the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill, the Redistribution and the estimates. The Grand Trunk Pacific Bill and the Redistribution have not yet come before us. The important departments of the Minister of Railways and the Minister of the Interior have not yet been touched. Now, Mr. Chairman, I am going to ask the Minister of Finance who is leading the House and who comes from one of the outlying districts, to say to his followers :	All right gentlemen, if you must go home on Friday evening or Friday morning, we will adjourn at six o'clock.

I cannot agree with my hon. friend's conclusions, though I may sympathize with much of his reasoning. I do not think lie is in a position to throw any stones at the province of Quebec. The province of Ontario has a larger representation than the province cf Quebec, and if you count the members you will find that the province of Ontario, that sends the largest number of gentlemen to either side of the House, is not much better represented in proportion than the province of Quebec. Therefore, the hon. gentleman should not single out Quebec in respect to the absentees. There are always a few faithful Tories and a few good Liberals present to attend to the business. But. I sympathize with what my hon. friend said in regard to members being absent not only

on Friday night, but sometimes on other nights. We are not much better off on Mondays than we are on Fridays. But, I cannot agree that that is a reason why we should not do any business on Friday night. There are only three, or perhaps four, days in the week during which we can have a full attendance, and if we are not to do any business except on those days we will be'here till October next. In regard to what my hon. friend said about three sessions a day, I have not heard any resolve on the part of the government to have three sessions a day, but I must say that I would rather have three sessions a day than adjourn on Friday. As to the question of government business, there has not been a session within my experience, and I have no doubt within the experience of other hon. gentlemen, when the government business has been more ready for the House than it has been at this session. There has never been a moment when there was not ample business to engage the attention of the House. In regard to the statement of my hon. friend that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) and the hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mi*. Sifton) have not asked for anything, the complaint is, on the other hand, that we have been asking too much. When we bring on the estimates we are told we must bring on Bills, and when we bring on Bills we are told that we are afraid to face the opposition by moving supply and that, therefore, we bring on Bills. It is exceedingly hard to please hon. gentlemen opposite. It seems that whatever we do is wrong. I want to appeal to my hon. friend-he and I come from those outlying parts of Canada ; we belong to the faithful few who are here day and night-whether the best way to punish the absentees is not to stay and go on with the work so that they will lose the opportunity of participating in the discussion. Seriously, I am quite sure my hon. friend cannot ask this item to he held over simply because he has misunderstood an observation made by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture.

The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) has found fault with hon. members representing Quebec for being absent on Friday night and he says he is here because he cannot get away. I do not think he should find fault. It is the members who can get away that are away.

The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) during the past couple of weeks, has been almost entirely absent from the House. Doing what ? Is it not an awkward situation for him to be in to be lecturing other hon. members for being away when he has been absent for two weeks ?

I have not been absent for two weeks, or one week. The statement I made is correct, and I think I have a right to protest in the manner I have done. Nothing that the hon. Minister of Finance has said has relieved the situation so far as the real business for which we were brought here is concerned. Tile three important questions that we were brought to this House to consider have not yet been brought to the attention of the House, notwithstanding the late day at which the session was called. I still have to say that if we are to be treated as we have been treated in the face of the absence of so many members we should not be expected to sit until the early hours of the morning.
You are not accustomed to going to bed early.
I understand all that. If we are to be treated in this way we should not be forced to sit on Friday evening and to continue until the early hours of the morning.
The hon. gentleman is addressing the wrong audience. Instead of scolding those present he should try to get an audience of the absentees and read that lecture to them.
My hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) is not making any mistake, because this same thing prevails in church. It is only those who are there that get the lecture.
I hope you are not insinuating that the hon. member for Macdonald belongs to that congregation.

At page D-26 of the Auditor General's Report I find this item :
Alex. Carder, Winnipeg, mounted heads and birds used for decoration,$1,015.
Would the hon. gentleman give us an explanation as to how these were selected, and by whom ?
They were selected in the same way as the Egan collection was for the Paris exhibition, and they were sent from Paris to Glasgow. I believe they are now in the High Commissioner's office.

The minister states that this collection of birds and heads together with the collection which was made at Halifax was sent from one exhibition to the other in the old country. I wish to take exception to that system of exhibiting specimens from Canada. I would like the hon. minister to give us a statement as to what classes of goods were sent from one exhibition to the other in the old country and whether he proposes to follow the same system at the St. Louis exhibition. If he does the people who attend and see the Canadian exhibit, will come to the conclusion that we have just one set of samples, and that we send it around to exhibitions in the same way as the ladies show their quilts at the fall fairs. If the hon. minister wishes to make a creditable display at the St. Louis exhibition, he should not get the exhibit up

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: out of old exhibits, but he should make a new selection even if it costs a little more money. Notwithstanding what the hon. minister has stated, I wish to say that I think that some agreement should be entered into between the government and the manufacturers whereby the government could expend a large amount of money in the preparation of a building so that they might be able to make an exhibition of Canadian goods within the Canadian building. I should like the hon. minister to make a statement that whatever furnishings are purchased in connection with the St. Louis exhibition will be Canadian goods. It would be well to make a Canadian gold exhibit, that if $491 is to be paid out of the Canadian, treasury it shall be paid to some Canadian, rather than to Mr. Treadgold, who lives in the old country. In looking at the detailed expenditure in connection w'itli the Paris exhibition, I find that there are thousands of dollars paid to people living in the old country for the furnishings that were put in the Canadian building. There could not be a better opportunity of exhibiting Canadian goods than to take Canadian goods over there even if it cost more money. The building in itself, if it is Canadian, will represent Canadian shingles on the roof. Canadian siding, Canadian furniture, and even printing material. All this will stand for Canada and show the people what we are doing in the way of manufacturing, &c. The minister has stated that he will consult the Live Stock Association as to that exhibit, and he might very well consult with other representative bodies as regards other exhibits. It would save a great deal of expense if he did so and it would result in a much more creditable exhibit on the part of Canada.

A large industrial buildin.g will be erected in St. Louis in which all the manufactured goods will have to be exhibited under the rules, so that the Canadian building will not be for exhibition purposes but will be furnished and arranged so as to illustrate Canadian products. For instance, there would be no use taking Canadian nails to use in the erection of the building. If we drove them into the boards on the floor they would make no sort of an exhibit, and if I can get nails in St. Louis at one-third the price of buying them here and sending them there it would be folly not to buy them in St. Louis. I hope of course to have a splendid exhibit of Canadian nails at St. Louis and I merely use that as an illustration of what I mean.

If the minister has an exhibition of Canadian nails he might use some of them in the construction of the building. In my humble opinion every particle of the material used in the Canadian building at St. Louis should be of Canadian product. If the employees could say that everything in the building was manufactured or grown
in Canada it would be in the interest of Canada, and it would be a pride to Canadians and the friends of Canada who visit that exhibition. The minister cannot pretend to say that it has been the practice in the i>ast to use goods of Canadian manufacture, because at the Paris exhibition thousands and thousands of dollars worth of even furniture not of Canadian manufacture was purchased. In one case $1,000 was paid for carpets which were not of Canadian manufacture.
Was any portion of the expense of the Manitoba exhibit at the Pan-American exhibition borne by this government ?

All we did with regard to the provincial exhibits was to facilitate their arrangement through our commissioner. The Dominion government did not make a special exhibit at the Pan-American beyond the decorative exhibits of the Canadian building.

Has the minister made any general remarks on the benefits of these exhibitions to Canada and more particularly the Japan exhibition, which he has had the pleasure of attending, and which prevented his presence here during the ei^ly part of the session ? It would be of interest to the House if the minister told us about that.
Do you not think it would be too bad for the absent members to miss that lecture ?
It might have the effect of punishing them for not being present.
This is the first question that has been put to me in regard to this exhibition. I will not at this late hour of the evening detain the House at very great length.
If the minister proposes to speak at some length, I would not ask him at this late hour of the night. He might do so on some other occasion.

I do not think there would be any other opportunity for it, but I may tresspass on the patience of the House to say a word or two with regard to our opportunities and the hopes for trade with the empire of Japan. I suppose I may say that I am myself personally responsible for the fact that we took part in that exhibition. For many years I have been reading about and studying the orient and the question of transpacific trade. I felt that in the future, I believed in the near future, there would be an enormous expansion of trade between this continent and the continent of Asia. Believing that, I have been looking into the progress of the nations on the other side of the Pacific ; and it seems to me that

there was every indication, from the enormous development of Japan during the past sixty years, since the revolution there, of a most magnificent trade between the western coast of this continent, and even the eastern part of this country, and the orient, especially the empire of Japan. Japan is a densely populated country, with over 40,000,000 people, very thickly settled in a country which can hardly feed them, even under the old conditions, when their food was of the simplest character. They are how opening their gates to foreign countries, and they are adopting the methods of an enormous industrial development. Heretofore, their industries have been what are called home industries, the people doing their work in their own homes or in small workshops. They are now establishing enormous factories and works all over the country according to the method of occidental nations, and consequently the people are being taken away from the production of food to these industrial centres. As an illustration, I may mention that the city of Osaka, where the exhibition was held, increased in population in the last four years from 700,000 people to over 1,000,000, the city of Tokio increased in the last ten years from 700,000 or 800,000 to 1,500,000, and the population of Japan has increased in the course of the fust ten years by over 5,000,000. The result is that the people of Japan can no longer feed themselves ; and, as they ask for better food and more of it, they must go abroad for that food. Up to the present time our American neighbours have had practical control of the market there. It lias not been an extremely large market. They have not been asking greatly for foreign food ; but now they are doing so, and I believed that it was very important that Canada should make an entry into that market in this early stage of its development and show what we could do in competition witli our neighbours. Therefore I urged on my colleagues the importance of making an exhibit in Japan, and I rejoice to say that the result of that exhibit and of my observations there has most amply justified that view. I believed that the best things for us to exhibit in Japan were the class of goods which seemed most likely to find a market there. Flour is one of the chief articles of trade between America and Japan. Heretofore what Is called Oregon or Washington flour has held the complete market there. That is very far inferior to our Canadian flour, not only in quality, but in strength to make bread ; and I was quite sure that any intelligent people who could see the bread made from Canadian flour, and how much more could he made from a barrel of Canadian flour than from a barrel of Pacific coast American flour, would be glad to get our flour.
There were tests made at the exhibition, I suppose ?

We made tests years ago. We have known for years that Canadian flour contained a much greater proportion of gluten than any other flour in the world, especially than the flour made from the soft wheats grown in the United States. Knowing that, I asked Mr. Hutchison, who is himself an old miller of long experience, to have comparative investigations made or the flour sent from the United States, and the flour that we would send. We were so satisfied with the results of that investigation that we felt convinced that a special exhibit of the qualities of Canadian flour at the exhibition would yield good results. WTe not only arranged to send an exhibit of flour, hut appliances for baking, and we had bread baked in the exhibition from Canadian flour. The result was one of the most enormous successes in the whole exhibition. People were simply wild and crazy to get samples of the bread. We had orders from hotels and restaurants throughout Osaka, who agreed to take all the bread that we could give them. We gave it to them on condition that they would state on their bills of fare that it was Canadian bread made from Canadian flour. We were able to supply them with bread of a quality such as they had never seen before. The result of the exhibit is that we have been already besieged with orders for Canadian flour, and I am glad to know that two of the great milling companies have arranged to send special agents to Japan. I may say in this connection that while we have done that, Canada will not reap the benefit of that expenditure and work unless the men engaged in the business in this country will make the necessary sacrifices to push their trade in the face of the energy and activity of their rivals in the United States. As confirmation of what I say, I may state that in American journals there have been letters from Americans in Japan most sever-ly criticising the government of the United States because it allowed Canada to get ahead of it in the way we did at the Osaka exhibition. I have been most gratified at the result of this exhibit. Not only for our western farmers and millers, but even fot eastern Canada there is to-day, as a direct result of the exhibition we made there, a market for an enormous trade in flour, in the empire of Japan, in China, and in the whole orient ; because visitors from China, Hong Kong, Manilla, the Straits Settlements and Singapore, were at that exhibition, and were all attracted by our Canadian exhibits and the excellence of the arrangement. On the very day that I sailed from Japan, the first of May last, a special messenger was sent from Osaka to Yokohama to present to Mr. Hutchison, who came with me, a medal for the best arranged and most artisticallj designed exhibit at the exhibition. That was awarded to the Canadian exhibit by the unanimous voice of the jury of awards for the whole exhibition, and it has been

brought here and placed in the department as a trophy of our victory. I have spoken of this flour exhibit. It was, however, only one of several. In addition to that, I venture to say that there is also a good chance for developing a large market for lumber and all the products of the forest in Japan. Japan is a forest country, but the demand for lumber is increasing and its forests are becoming exhausted. I was rather disgusted, I must confess, to And first-class Canadian lumber sold as Oregon pine. The people took for granted that it came from the United States, and it was handled by the merchants of Seattle, Takoma and Portland, and not by the merchants of Victoria and Vancouver to any great extent. If our lumbermen from the western provinces will only undertake to push their goods in that market, there is abundant scope there for a large and profitable trade. Among other things we showed was a small furniture exhibit. When we were arranging the exhibit, the Consul General of Japan advised us to rent a furnished house as there was not much accommodation at the hotel for European and American travellers, and in that connection I may say that the Japanese methods of living and the arrangements of their houses are entirely foreign to us and very inconvenient and uncomfortable.
Occasionally they are described as picturesque.

Yes, but not comfortable. We did not succeed in renting a house, and my commissioner made arrangement with a hotel to take our people on a reasonable basis. This furniture was put on exhibition and attracted a good deal of attention. We could have sold it fifty times over at prices that would have given plenty profit after paying all the charges, duty and commission. To-day that furniture is all sold to people of prominence who were eager to get it and to show it as a trophy of the Canadian exhibit, and it will be an advertisement of Canadian furniture for a long time to come. I have been urging the same organization which sent furniture to the Buffalo exhibition to immediately send an agent to Japan, and if they do they will get a large trade of a most profitable character. We also had another exhibit of pulp and paper which ought to result in a large trade. It may be rather new to many people that the Japanese are extremely fond of newspapers, and that there is an enormous press circulation there. They get all their paper from Europe and I believe that a great deal of it is made from Canadian pulp, which is sent to England and France and then exported to Japan in the shape of paper. In the city of Osaka, there are two newspapers with a circulation each of over a 100,000 daily, besides a large number of newspapers with even greater circulations. We had an exhibit of pulp in its different stages of
manufacture as well as the raw wood and the different kinds of paper made from it in Canada. This attracted great attention and many inquiries, and if to-day our paper and pulp manufacturers can meet the demand, they will find a large market in Japan. We had in addition a cold storage exhibit of our fruits, which excited great interest. There is undoubtedly a market in Japan for British Columbia green fruit. In that respect Japan is rather backwards. They grow very little of the fruits we are accustomed to. They have cherry trees without cherries, plum trees without plums, and peach trees without peaches. We hear a great deal of the cherry trees of Japan, but they are grown from blossoms and have no fruit, and the same may be said of their plums and peaches. They have been growing apples in recent years in the northern part of the island, which were introduced from Europe and America, and are doing so most successfully, but they cannot meet the demand of the people for fresh fruit. Our British Columbians can send over there fresh fruit to large extent and find a good market. Canned meats, fruits and vegetables would also find ready sale. In salmon there is already a considerable export from British Columbia and that trade is steadily increasing. Under these circumstances there is evidently a great opening for trade with Japan. The ordinary labouring class there are getting better wages 'than ever before and they are beginning to understand European and American ways of living; they are asking for the thing used by us. The Americans are active in the propaganda of their own trade, and if we are to reap the advantages to be derived from an exhibition of this kind, our people must wake up and push their work. Trade is not going to fall into our mouths while we lie on our backs. The people who want to take advantage of the Japanese market must wake up.
Has the hon. gentleman any suggestion to make as to any particular step we should take ?

The first thing is for us to send our agents there. Our furniture organization ought to send our agents, so ought our paper mills. Our smaller industries could combine together and send out agents. They should do so at once, and as the name of Canada gets better known there will be more and more trade to be done and better facilities for doing it. I may say to my hon. friend that until this exhibition took place, there were scarcely any people in Japan who knew of the existence of Canada. Everything that came from the American continent was credited to the United States, even in the case of goods from British Columbia. British Columbia was not known to Japan except as a country which tried to legislate against the Japanese. I may

tell my hon. friend that the chief difficulty I had in dealing with the people there was the fact that British Columbia was attempting to legislate against the Japanese. The Japanese are proud and rather sensitive. They are a nation in the sense of coming lately into the comity and family of a nation of the world though their civilization extends back a thousand years. Amongst the people of the western world they are a young nation, and they are proud of the fact that recently they have been accepted as the ally of the British empire and have been received among the civilized nations of the world. They resent extremely the idea of being classed with the barbarian Chinese, and of having any special legislation against them in any country with which they are asked to trade, I say this because it is the only one thing that interfered in any way with the desire on the part of the Japanese to trade and to open up more friendly and more extended relations with us. X may say that, in consequence of the fact that I was a minister of the Crown here-partially at all events, but not altogether perhaps, because the exhibit had been arranged before I reached there and the impression had been largely created-I was received with the greatest cordiality and courtesy by everybody. Every facility was placed at my disposal to present the views and ideas of Canada, and every opportunity to let the people know what we had to sell and how we could open and improve the trade there.
Did the hon. gentleman deliver any addresses in Japan ?

I was entertained at three or four banquets, and spoke at them, dwelling a little upon these matters. That was not, however, the only or the most important fact. Perhaps it is a little difficult for "us in this matter of fact country to understand the point of view of the oriental mind. They are a people of ceremony, a people very largely impressed with titles. And when the Minister of Agriculture from Canada was received by the Minister of Foreign Affairs or entertained by the government of the country or presented personally at a special audience to the Emperor and Empress, that created an impression amongst these people which we here can hardly appreciate or understand, because we do not think so much of these things as the people in the orient do. These facts were circulated all through the country, and people who had never heard of Canada before began to ask where Canada was and what it was. Then, I must say that the authorities at the exhibition and everybody connected with it, were most kind and courteous, and gave us every facility, if I may say so, to advertise our wares and our country. In that way, perhaps, an impression

was created greater than could have been created in any other way. I know that Americans and Europeans travelling through the country were immensely impressed with what Canada had done. They were astonished, and not only did they congratulate us, but they went so far as to criticise and condemn their own governments for having let slip an opportunity of which Canada had taken the greatest advantage. I am afraid I have rather wearied the House by speaking so long on the subject. But personally I believe there is a great deal in it, I am satisfied that great benefit will accrue to Canada through the expenditure made in this service, if the people wilio are engaged in the lines of trade affected will take it up and push it now while the impression that Canada has made is fresh in the Japanese mind, and when they can do the best work.
Did the hon. gentleman come to any conclusion as to the future of the industrial life and activity started in Japan in its effect as to the export of the manufactures of that country V

I watched that very closely and investigated it as far as the time at my disposal would allow. I spoke, a few moments ago of the fact that only recently the industrial production of Japan was what might be called home industry. That system of production results in individuality of product, but not in uniformity. They have now adopted the factory system in textiles and in all matters of iron production. In some other respects, they have refused to adopt that system. As a matter of fact, the government found that the change was so rapid and produced such crucial effects that it was almost shaking the foundations of their society. Therefore, a check has been deliberately put by the authorities upon the change that was taking place in the direction of adopting the factory system. In their factory production we see the effects of the old training. A thousand pieces of cotton turned out by a Japanese factory are not so perfect or so uniform as a thousand pieces turned out by one of our factories. The old inherent quality still remains with tile present generation of their people, and I think it will be some time before you can get as uniform and as generally perfect production as those of our old established industries and well-trained operatives. I think it will probably be a generation or two before Japan can reach that point. At the same time she is making great progress in that direction, producing great quantities of goods, which, though not quite as good as can be produced in the United States or England or Canada, still are fairly good. I do not believe that Japan is going to enter into competition with the occidental nations in the market of the world for some time to come. But there

are certain lines of goods that we cannot sell them now. Cotton we sent. Silk goods, of course, we cannot pretend to send. They make the best silk goods in the world, and send out large quantities, this being the largest article of their trade. Iron goods we cannot sell to them. They make wonderful tools, with marvellous temper and edge, and In ordinary castings, &c., they have been very successful in adapting themselves to the American and European methods of production. They show wonderful facilities in organizing new industries. I visited several of these and w'as astonished to find great establishments employing thousands of operatives, without a single European or American among them; organized from top to bottom by Japanese, managed by Japanese, the work-people all Japanese, and turning out-especially in the iron industry-most excellent work. When I say most excellent work, I do not say that it is quite up to the best work in America and Europe, but still very good work. I had the opportunity of visiting a large ship-building yard in the town of Kobe. At the head of it was a mao of about thirty-five, a graduate of Cambridge University. He had taken the scientific and engineering courses, and had spent seven years in Europe preparing for his work. Returning to Japan he organized this industry. The concern employs four thousand operatives, and has a most complete organization. He had organized a savings bank for his operatives, established reading rooms and museums, in short, had as complete and modern am organization as any I know of in Europe or America. That concern was completely organized and carried on by a Japanese, for Japanese, with Japanese capital. That is only one instance of many. For that reason, I have not dwelt so much on the general possibilities of trade in ordinary manufactures there. Still I am not prepared to say that there is no opportunity; I think there is in certain lines.

Before the hon. gentleman sits down, I would like to ask if he was able to make such observations of the social and economic conditions as would justify him in coming to a conclusion with respect to the effect that extensive emigration from Japan might have upon our conditions in Canada.

I am satisfied, in the first place, that there will be no such emigration from Japan. The Japanese are a home-loving people, and they have abundant opportunity for progress and industry in their own country. The Japanese government itself forbids the emigration of anybody from the country without a permit, and for several years past, they have refused to issue a permit to affy Japanese to come from Japan to Canada who is a labourer or of the ordinary labouring class. Permits are issued only to merchants, students and travellers.
Did that extend to emigration to any other country than Canada 1

The system extends to every country, no Japanese can leave his own country without a permit from his government. The government there, in accordance with negotiations with our government, have issued orders, I think, about two years ago, that for the future no permit should be given to a Japanese, except the classes I have mentioned, to go to Canada, and that has been strictly maintained to the present time. I had the assurance of the 'government there, personally and in writing, that that policy would be maintained.
My hon. friend spoke about the possibilities of industrial invasion. I consider that there is no prospect of that. The Japanese are a home-loving people, proud of their nation, proud of their empire, and a most devoted patriotism seems to inspire them from top to bottom of every class, men, women and children. The one thing that strikes a visitor is the intense and devoted patriotism of the Japanese for their own country. That means that they do not wish to leave it, they want to stay there. To be sure, some enterprising people go out, but generally speaking the people remain at home. They have now, with their industrial development, an abundant opportunity for labour in their own country, and consequently there is no great inducement for them to go out. Wages are improving, and they are satisfied apparently with their condition.
What is the hon. gentleman's opinion as to the articles of food now entering into general consumption by the masses ?

Among the articles of food they are going to take up first, will be bread. They ate rice before, and bread is beginning to take its place. The ordinary labourer uses bread only as a luxury, while the well-to-do people are beginning to eat it as we do. Flour therefore is the first thing. They are beginning to eat more meat, they do not produce much meat in that country. They have very few animals, so few as to be hardly noticeable. They eat a large quantity of fish, very good fish, and they have great fisheries. I believe there will be considerable trade with them in canned meat. I do not believe we can send mutton there, because the Australians are sending in large quantities, and we cannot compete with them. But we ought to be able to send beef there, and hog products. They are beginning to eat pork and bacon, although at first, when Europeans began to go there, they did not seem to care much for them. They have a good deal of poultry there, I

do not think we will be able to send much poultry or eggs for some time to come.
They have extensive fisheries of their own, I suppose ?
Yes, but still they buy considerable fish from British Columbia, and their purchases are increasing.
Have they any native dairy products ?

Practically none. We can send them butter and some cheese. I may say my department has been sending them butter for two or three years. But since I have been there the trade, I think, will decidedly improve. As a rule, however, they do not eat butter. They use a great deal of rape seed oil instead, for cooking. But as they begin to eat bread they will want butter with it.
What about their tariff regulations ?
They have got a low tariff.
What would be the duty on furniture ?

I think 10 per cent or 12 per cent; on flour about the same, but I am speaking from memory only. It is a decidedly low tariff, and we stand in the same position with respect to all these articles as everybody else. They have treaties with certain countries giving them the most-favoured-nation advantages which those countries give them on certain articles, but it happens that nearly all those articles are things we do not produce. Now, I wish to say to my hon. friend from Bothwell (Sir. Clancy) that I am ready to go back to the census item and to give him the information that he asked for.

It is so late now I think we had better stop. * I am sure we are all very much indebted to the hon. gentleman for the very interesting account he has given us of the exhibition and the people of Japan.

I do not want to be unreasonable, but in the early part of the evening the hon. member for Bothwell refused to let me go on with the census item because I had not certain information. I have that information now, and I would like to give it.
I do not object to the Information but there is a great deal more that the committee will want to get.

I have asked my officers to stay here and get this information, and I propose to give it to the committee. The hon. gentleman Hon. Mr. FISHER.
wanted information as to the questions asked in the schedules of the census of 1S91 and of 1901. In schedule 3, are questions relating to houses and constructions, houses inhabited and houses uninhabited. These are in schedule 2 of 1901, but were not in the schedules of 1891.
