limit of time in 1891. If his parents or friends answered that he intended to be away less than a year, then he was counted as being a resident.
If there was a family of four living in Ottawa and the enumerator found that three had been absent for nine months in Chicago working, they would be taken down as residents of Ottawa ?
Yes, if it were stated by the parent or person giving information that they had not been absent more than a year and were considered as residents of Ottawa.
In that case the census would not be correct ?
No de jure census is absolutely correct in that sense. Of course these people would have to say their absence was only temporary.

I see that in the town of Paris, county of Brant, Mr. Kent charges for horse-hire $10.50. Mr. Wilson charges precisely the same, while Mr. Iloey does not charge anything, but charges $3.50 for expenses. Mr. Shannon charges $10.50 for horse-hire, Mr. McCammon $9 and Mr. A. W. Rousell $10.50. There seems to be a general agreement fixing the charge at $10.50. There is uniformly $9 charged for instructions.
They drew $9 each because the commissioner kept them three days giving instructions.
How does there come to be this uniformity in regard to horse-hire ?

I suppose the men had to pay about the same price to go over the same distance with their horses. If they went from Paris to Brantford, I presume the price would be the same for one as for the other.
Mi\ CLANCY. We are not asking for the hon. gentleman's supposition. Why not produce the accounts ?
I have explained that so often, I do not think it is necessary.

The hon. gentleman ought to give a better reason than that it is not convenient for him to do so. 1 will take the case here of Mr. Hoey. Mr. IToey does not get anything for horse-hire. How did the others get it, while he does not get it V Mr. Hoey gets $3.50 for expenses. What were the expenses in that case ?

I explained a little while ago that if the charges amounted to more than $3 a day they could not be allowed. Mr. Hoey's charges may have amounted to more than $3
a day and consequently he could not be paid for horse-hire, or Mr. Hoey may possibly have driven with one of the other enumerators from Paris to Brantford and not have charged for it. I cannot tell the reason myself. The only way would be to ask Mr. Hoey why he did not charge for horse-hire.

The hon. gentleman knows that their earnings must appertain to the recording, so that it did not arise in that way. I have just pointed out a case where one enumerator got $23, another $20, another $29, another $27, another $26 and another $38. I am presuming that the populations in that case were not the same in different polling subdivisions and therefore- the differences would arise there. But, the other must have been for horse-hire actually used by each of them and the instructions must have been uniform. We have paid the enumerators $3 a day while getting their instructions. What were the instructions on that point ?

A special allowance was made for the time spent in receiving instructions of $3 a day. Apparently nearly all of the enumerators in Brant county spent three days receiving instructions. One of them appears to have been absent part of the time and consequently he did not charge for three days.

What were the instructions given the recorder in regard to how they should be paid as to the days employed taking instructions and the days they were employed enumerating? When they were at the work of enumeration they were not to earn more than $3 a day. What instructions were given to the enumerators as to how they should be paid. for their services ? The chief commissioner is sitting there and he could tell the hon. gentleman and the hon. gentleman could probably read the instructions to the committee. Was any alteration made in regard to the allowances made to the enumerators from the first intimation they had.
There was no alteration made after the first table of allowances.

There were complaints in the newspapers'that the minister had misled them as to the amount of compensation. If a man went to a farmhouse and asked a number of. questions it should not cost much more expense than if he asked a dozen questions. Many of these schedules are worthless if they are ever to be used. We have for the first time a record of divorces. That is rather a delicate question. Did the enumerator put that question to the minister himself ? Does lie think that such a thing as that should be put on record ? Some of this is the most trashy stuff that ever went to the country. How many vol-

umes will there be in this census and the number of pages ?

The first volume has already been issued) and the matter for the second volume is, almost ready for the printer. If we put only the information in the second volume that was in the second volume of 1891 it would be ready now.
Will all these tables be published.
Certainly.
When will the part containing information with regard to the industries be ready ?
I expect it will be ready for the printers in a little over a month.
If I remember rightly, it was out in 1892. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman why that has been so long delayed, so much longer than it was in 1891 ?

The hon. gentleman is not correct in his statement. The third volume of the census of 1891, which contained the returns of manufactures, was issued on the 20th of February, 1895. I expect that the returns of the industries of Canada will be out in July, 1903, or about twenty months earlier than those of the census of 1891.

I spoke somewhat subject to correction. I heartily congratulate the hon. gentleman upon being right for once. How did he take the census, say, of the district of Alberta and the other outlying districts of the country-the Indians and so on?
The census of the Indians was generally taken by the officers of the Indian Department.
How is the population taken in Alaska and in the country around Hudson's Bay V

So far as I know, the population of Alaska was taken by the census commissioners of the United States. With regard to the districts around Hudson's Bay and the other unorganized territories, we sent some of our own commissioners for that purpose.
How does our progress compare with that of the United States and the mother country in the compilation and publication of the census returns ?

Our census is taken a year after that of the United States ; but independently of that, I think our census is not quite as far ahead as that of the United States in compilation. We have not so large a staff, even in pro-Mr. CLANCY.
portion to the area of the country, as they have.
Do they not use some mechanical devices for the purpose of tabulation ?

Yes, very largely. We discussed that point, and came to the conclusion, and it was the experience in 1891, that it would take so long to train people to do the work, and the machines are so very expensive, that it would involve more loss than gain to use them.
I have read descriptions of their work, which seems to be wonderful.

That is quite true. Some years ago, when I was in Washington, I visited the Census Bureau and saw the working of these machines, and Mr. Blue, the chief census commissioner, went down there to see what was best to be done. These machines have been of great value in expediting the work of the American census, but for a small work such as ours is in comparison with theirs, we made up our minds, for the reasons stated, that it would not be advisable to adopt these machines. I may say, however, that we use six adding machines. As a general rule, the permanent employees do more of the intellectual work in connection with the census than the work of compilation.
It is purely mechanical ?
For a person who is an expert it is.
Are they very expensive ?
About $1,500 a machine.

I called the attention of the hon. minister two years ago to the fact that the cost of taking the census had been largely increased in the province of Prince Edward Island. I also called his attention to the fact that one Doyle, who was appointed enumerator, had sold out his job to another man named Broderick for $30, and Broderick was appointed in the place of Doyle. Did that $30 come out of Broderick's pocket, or was it paid by the department ?
There was no money paid to Doyle by the department. Broderick was appointed from here in Doyle's place on the recommendation of Sir Louis Davies.

The amount paid Broderick was twice that paid the enumerator in 1891, and one would judge therefore that the payment to Doyle by Broderick came indirectly from the. department. It may be that the increases generally in the

cost of taking the census was due to matters of that kind. Two years ago 1 brought the matter before the House, and the hon. minister said he would make an inquiry and give me the information I desired, hut none has been forthcoming yet. I have seen both the men since. All that Doyle would say was that he had $30 in his pocket for doing very little work. In all the other districts increases have taken place, despite the fact that the population of the island was 5,000 souls less In 1901 than it was in 1891. What is the explanation of that ?

I can only repeat the explanation I have given already. A great many more questions were asked, and more time had to be spent by the enumerators. As I pointed out a few minutes ago, three questions were asked in 1901 for every question asked in 1891, in round figures. That took more time and the enumerators had to be paid more. Again, the whole scale of wages and of living is higher than in 1891, and people would not work at the same pay. Consequently we were compelled to make allowances for horse-hire and for the time spent in receiving instructions and returning schedules. These taken together make up the difference.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) I presume, has taken a fair census in the province of Prince Edward Island. He will notice that there has been a decrease in population there, and, in consequence, the province is losing one representative in this parliament. I would ask the hon. gentleman if the same system of taking the census was followed in the province of Quebec and in the province of Prince Edward Island. This is a very important question in connection with our representation.
Exactly the same system was employed all over Canada.
Did not the hon. minister refer to the cures for information ?
What does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) mean ? I asked the same question of everybody in the province.

Did not a certain Mr. CotS issue a circular to the priests of the province of Quebec asking for a return with regard to the census taken by the priest in that year, and was not our census largely based on the returns made by the clergymen ?

Certainly not. The enumeration taken by the parish priests of the province of Quebec was obtained only after the census returns were made up and complete. It was obtained for the sake of comparison and information, but our schedules were not
changed in any consequence of that information.

That is somewhat different from the statement we had two years ago, when we were told by the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) himself that this means of taking the census in Quebec had been resorted to because of the timidity of the people of the province with regard to census enumeration. When approached by the enumerator they imagined that it was a matter of additional taxation, and were afraid to answer the questions asked by the enumerators. In consequence of that, Mr. Cote, the assistant commissioner, issued a circular to each of the Roman Catholic priests of the province of Quebec asking them for a return of parties who had left the province in their respective parishes, not only those who had left temporarily but those who had left intending to remain away. So, parties who had left the parish within the year were enumerated as residents of the province. If that was the system adopted in the province of Quebec, it must have had the effect of increasing the unit of representation, and relatively depreciating the enumeration in the province of Prince Edward Island. I have not time at the present, it being a little early in the morning, to refer to ' Hansard,' of 1901, yet, if the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fisher) will take the trouble to read it, he will find that his leader made the statement I have just referred to. The Cote circular was sent not only to the parish priests of the province of Quebec, but it was sent to certain clergymen in Prince Edward Island in the districts where there was known to be a French population. The Rev. Dr. Ohas-son, of Palmer Road parish, where there is a large Acadian population, received a copy, and so did the Rev. Mr. Gallant, of Bloomfield, another gentleman at Itustico and Father Boudreault, at Egmont Bay. The Rev. Dr. Chasson was the only one to reply to the circular, and, as he said, he did not think it right that the priests should interfere in the census in any respect, but should leave it to the enumerators and the people. Now the taking of the census in Prince Edward Island in 1901 cost a hundred per cent more than the taking of the census in 1891. I find no fault with the census on the ground of correctness; it may have been correct. But it has resulted in showing a falling off of 5,000 people in the province of Prince Edward Island. While the schedules with regard to nationality, race, religion and other matters were strictly applied in the province of Prince Edward Island, yet, it would seem that a different system was applied in the province of Quebec, the pivotal province, upon which rests,the representation from all the provinces of Canada. I wish the hon. gentleman to be definite and say whether his leader, the Prime Minister, was incorrect when, in 1901, he made the statement I have

repeated to you. But if the Cote circular was distributed as tbe first minister stated and the enumeration of the people of the province of Quebec was based upon that circular, I say that a gross injustice has been done to the people of Prince Edward Island. The highest privilege of any people is the exercise of the franchise for the election of representatives to parliament, and that sacred right should not be tampered with. I would ask the minister to make it perfectly clear whether this right has been tampered with or whether the same system has applied to Prince Edward Island that was applied to Quebec. I believe that if the system had been the same, there would not have been shown a decrease of 5,000 in Prince Edward Island, with the resultant loss of one member in this House, but a large increase. I ask the hon. gentleman to make a clear statement because the people of Prince Edward Island are very much excited over the loss of one representative in this parliament.
It should be fully stated in this parliament whether the same system of counting the people has been applied to the province of Prince Edward Island as was applied to the province of Quebec.

Absolutely the same system, the same regulations in every respect were carried out in every province. The circulars the hon. gentleman refers to, one of them was sent out for the purpose of asking the priests, not only in Quebec but wherever there was a French population, to explain to the people that they must give full and ample information to the enumerators. The other circular was sent out to make certain inquiries in regard to the number of people in each parish who were away to stay away, so that they would not be improperly counted. The people who were not coming back were not to be counted. It was desirable to check the work. But the replies to that circular were never put into the hands of the compilers here, and were only compared with the schedules by the superior officers, and the result was no change in the schedule returns.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if this circular was sent out to the clergymen of any other denomination in Canada at that time ?
No.

Then it was simply confined to the province of Quebec, and a few circular letters were sent to the parish priests in the parish of Prince Edward Island ?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE, No, it was sent to others besides.
To which of the other provinces was the circular sent 5
To all the French districts all over Canada.
Sent exclusively then to the French districts ?
Yes.
There was some reason then for sending out that circular. He says it was sent out to receive information for the purpose of checking the work done by his sworn officials ?

The first circular was sent out for the purpose of asking the parish priests to impress upon their people the necessity of answering freely. It is well known that among the French population of the country there was more or less fear with regard to the answers to the census enumerators, and this expedient was adopted to remove that fear. The second circular was sent out, as I have explained, because it was understood that a large number of French Canadians who had gone away to the United States, and we wished to check the numbers of those who had gone there to settle and not confuse them with those who had gone there temporarily.

So it was sent especially for the purpose of ascertaining the number of French Canadians who had left Canada in previous years and gone to the United States ?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE, That was the purpose.

Then why should the hon.. gentleman endeavour to keep the run of, the French Canadian people any more than the English speaking people of Canada ? .1 cannot see why he should incur this extra expense for the purpose of ascertaining the drift, the current, or the movements of the French people in the province of Quebec, when the same thing had not been done with regard to the English speaking people of the other provinces. I say there must be a deeper reason than that. The hon. gentleman appears not inclined to answer that question. It is a question that affects the sacred rights of the people of Prince Edward Island and their right of representation in this parliament, and I insist that the hon. gentleman answer it. When he adopted such a mode of counting the people of Quebec, the province that fixes the unit of representation in the other provinces, in justice and fair-play to the other provinces, the same means should have been taken to count the English speaking people of Canada.
In consequence of this, I believe that in Quebec, according to the hon. gentleman's

own statement, ascertaining the current of immigration from Canada to the United States, they counted thousands of people in Quebec who had left during the previous year that were not counted in the other provinces of Canada, and as a result of this unfair system of counting the people of Prince Edward Island are asked to submit to the loss of representatives in this parliament. I would like to have a definite reply from the hon. minister, if he found it necessary in order to have a f-air count of the people to issue this circular, why he did not send a similar document to the clergymen of other denominations in order to ensure a fair count of the English speaking people.

The same circular in regard to the French population was sent all over the Dominion. The hon. gentleman has asked another question. There was not a single name added to the list of the population of Quebec as a result of the answers which came in reply to that circular.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if he authorized the issue of the circular which was sent to the curds of Quebec?
The hon. gentleman asks me if I authorized it. I cannot say I gave any orders to have it issued.
When did the hon. minister learn of the purpose for which it was issued ?
I knew about it, but did not see the circular before it was issued.
I will read what the hon. minister said in the House of Commons in 1901. Mr. Barker was speaking :

I would like to ask the hon. minister 11 he is aware that Mr. Cfltd has issued another circular, one that is quite as improper, apparently, as the .one issued in Ontario, in which he asks that returns be made direct to him as assistant commissioner of matters wholly outside his duty as commissioner ? Does the hon. minister know that Mr. Cdte has asked to have returns made to him of French Canadians who do not live in this country at all, but who live in the United States ?
I will answer the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Barker's) question first. I am not aware of such a circular as the hon. gentleman indicates.
My bon. friend is now referring to the second circular. The answer.I gave a few minutes ago was in regard to the first circular.
That cannot be possible. It is impossible. The hon. gentleman says that he knew of the circular issued to the curds before it was issued.
Pardon me. What I said a few minutes ago was
What the hon. minister states now is that he knew of the circular before it was issued.
Which circular ?
The second circular.
I did not state so.

The hon. minister stated so a few minutes ago. Two years ago his recollection should have been much better when he stated that he did not know of the issue of such a circular. Now, he is in direct contradiction of himself. He says he did know. The first circular did not refer to the French population at all. The first circular that was brought to the attention of the hon. minister was brought to his notice by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett). This was the circular brought to his notice in 1901, and it was issued apparently for the purpose of getting political information.
The MINISTER OF 'AGRICULTURE. I have made no reference to that circular to-night.

During the discussion of the question of the circular issued to the French cures, the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) asked the question :
I would like to ask the hon. minister if he is aware that Mr. C6td has issued another circular. one that is quite as improper, apparently, as the one issued in Ontario, in which he asks that returns be made direct to him as assistant commissioner of matters wholly outside his duty as commissioner. Does the hon. minister know that Mr. C6td has asked to have returns made to him of French Canadians who do not live in this country at all, but who live in the United States ?
That is the French curds' circular.
What was my answer ?

The answer of the hon. minister was :
I will answer the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Barker's) question first. I am not aware of such a circular as the hon. gentleman indicates.
Exactly.
Just a few moments ago he said that he was aware.
I said I was not aware.
I understood the hon. minister to say he was aware.

I said that in regard to the circular issued to the parish priests of Quebec asking them

to impress upon their parishioners that they must give full information to the census enumerators which is another circular altogether. There were two circulars issued to the priests of Quebec, one before the enumeration asking them to get their parishioners to give full and complete returns, and another six months after the enumeration which the hon. gentleman has just referred to and in regard to which I answered Mr. Barker at that time.
I understand that there were at least three circulars issued by the Department of Agriculture.
There were two circulars issued. I know nothing of any other circular issued by the department or any officer of the department.
Two circulars were issued to the French cures ?
Yes.
Has that gentleman a copy of these circulars here ?
I have not got them here. They were laid on the Table of this House when the question was up before.

It seems to me that the hon. minister should lay on the Table of this House a copy of the circulars, because it is quite clear that there have been circulars Issued which are entirely outside of the usual understanding of what is the purpose and the work of the census commissioner.
They have been in possession of the House for more than a year.
What did the minister say as to the circular regarding political leanings.
No such circular was ever issued by my department.
When was the minister aware that such circular was issued ?
When I was informed of it later on.
What was done with that circular ?
I do not know.
Did the minister take any action in reference to that circular ?
When I heard of it I immediately gave instructions that such a circular had not been issued on my authority and that they must not pay attention to it.
Did the minister come into possession of copies of the circular?
It was read on the floor of parliament.
It was issued by some one in connection with the department.
It was not.
It was acted upon by certain enumerators and it evidently imposed on them. Did the minister take any steps to ascertain who they were who were guilty of what was practically a forgery.
My name was not forged to it.
Does the minister feel that he has done his whole duty in the matter ?
Yes.
If the minister holds such opinions I would not wonder if more of such circulars would be issued. How many schedules were issued in the census of 1901 ?
Fifteen.
How many questions were included in the first schedule ?

If the hon. gentleman had been here during the sitting, he would have heard the answers to the questions he is now asking, and I am afraid I shall have to refer him to ' Hansard ' if he asks any more questions about matters which have been discussed this afternoon. In the first schedule there were thirty-four questions.

I do not think there is any justification for the minister refusing to answer a question of a member because lie has been absent from the House for a time. Have all these thirty-four questions been answered ?
Yes.
How many questions were there in the second schedule ?
Twenty-five.
Have all these been answered ?
Yes.
How many questions in the third schedule ?
Fifteen.
What is the total number ?

The hon. gentleman can add up as correctly as I.
.TUNE 12, 1903

How many questions in the fourth schedule ?
The* MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. Seventeen.
How many questions in schedule number five.
Thirty-seven.
To what do these questions refer to.
To field products.

What field products ?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE, the field products usually grown in Canada.
I do not wish for a general answer by a detailed list.
I have read those questions in detail to the House and will not do it again.

I am sorry for the county of Pictou. This is the second time the hon. minister refuses to answer a question. Might I ask the hon. minister at what date these questions will be completed by the officers in his department ?
The compilation will be completed about the middle of next month.
How many schedules in all were asked ?
Fifteen.
Of these we learn that four have been compiled, and the hon. minister expects to have the compilation of all the schedules completed in the course of the year.
I said in the month of January next.

In seven months the hon. gentleman expects to complete the compilation of eleven schedules and it has taken his department twenty-four months to complete four, or an average of six months each. He now expects to complete the work of compiling eleven schedules in seven months.
The hon. gentleman shows that he has not been following the debate for his statements are not in accord with what has been said.

I must admit that, to a certain extent, I have not been following the debate, because I was not aware of the rare intellectual treat the chamber was having. I understood from the hon. gentleman that there are fifteen schedules. I understood further that his department has completed four. The census was taken in April, 1901, and we are now at the end of June. 1903. If has. therefore, taken twenty-four months to compile the answers to four questions, and the hon. minister expects to complete that whole work of compiling the census in Januafy, 1904. Now, from June, 1903. to January, 1904, is seven months. So, the hon. minister will find my estimate correct when I say that he expects to compile the answers to the eleven schedules in seven months, whereas it has taken him twenty-four months to compile the answers to four. If he impugns my accuracy, may I ask him on what ground ?
The hon. gentleman's statement as to four schedules is incorrect.
The hon. gentleman informed me that the fifth schedule is not completed. I inferred that four were completed. Perhaps that is not the impression that he intended to convey. Was I mistaken ?
The hon. gentleman is not accurate.
We shall have the opportunity of referring to ' Hansard ' in a few days to see what the hon. gentleman said.
The hon. gentleman asked me a question whether the answers to these four schedules were completed, and now he is asking about a compilation that I know nothing about.
Then we may begin over again. Have the answers to the fifth schedule been compiled ?
The compilation is not yet finished.
Have the answers with reference to the preceding four schedules been compiled ?
In some cases they have and in some they have not.

Then it appears that I was crediting the minister with too much when I said that the answers to four schedules had been compiled. Will he tell me how many of the six hundred odd questions in the schedules have been completed ?

Schedule 1, schedule 2 and schedule 3 have been compiled. Schedules 10 and 11 are also finished. In the rest the compilation is under way. Schedules 4, 5, 6 and 7 are verging towards completion, and schedule 8 will be completed before the end of next month.
What is the number of the schedule referring to manufactures ?
No. 8.
How many questions were in that schedule ?
Sixty-seven.
There was a limitation with respect to manufacturing establishments in the census of 1901 as compared with that of 1891. Will the hon. minister state what it is ?

In 1891 every room or shop in which one or two persons were employed was called a manufacturing establishment. In 1901 the rule was followed that five hands must be employed before an establishment could be considered a manufactory.
Can the hon. gentleman form any idea of the number of establishments that have been struck off the schedule by adopting the form of question he adopted for the census of 1901 ?

An establishment not having five working people in it is not taken as an establishment and could not be struck off. We have not reached any point in the compilation that will indicate a fair estimate of the difference brought about by this different mode of taking establishments.
How many questions were asked under schedule No. 6 ?
Twenty-six.

The twenty-six classes into which the live stock of Canada is divided
must include, I suppose, poultry ?
Yes.
Does it include the eggs of the farmers ?
Eggs are included in farm products.
Has a distinction been made between different breeds in this classification ?
There is a distinction made in the different breeds in pure bred stock but not in grade animals.
Does the hon. minister expect that this amount will complete the taking of the census and when will the second volume of the census be put before the public ?
It is expected that this amount will complete the compilation of the census and that the second volume will be issued before the end of next month.

The presence of four Cabinet Ministers in the Chamber this morning is the best proof that the Grand Trunk subsidy has been settled because there will apparently be no meeting of the Cabinet on this 13th day of June. My hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) who is Hon. Mr. FISHER.
not present in the Chamber now but who will be here in a few minutes, stated last night that we were going to have' three sessions of the House per day soon and although the Minister of Finance contradicted that the Minister of Agriculture seems bound to have an all day and an all night sitting too.
I find by the Public Accounts that the census of 1871 cost about $400,000. the census of 1881 considerably under $500,000, and the census of 1891, not much over the half million mark. I wrould ask the Minister of Agriculture what the present census has cost up to date ?
The expenditure up to June 1, 1903, was $1,137,533.37.
When the people see these figures, and compare them with the cost of previous censuses, they will be rather staggered. What further sum will it take to complete the taking of this census ?
I am asking for a vote of $35,000 for the ensuing year, and I suppose it will take about $8,000 for this month of June. They will make about $43,000 more.
Do I understand that when the amount is spent, it will complete the census in its entirety 7
Yes.

I should think the people will be rather thankful that the census is at an end. I think the minister should explain why this census has cost so much. I am going to give some of the reasons. First and foremost, I think it was due to his bringing Mr. Blue here as an officer of this department. Not that I lay anything to Mr. Blue personally ; but he had been a government officer in the province of Ontario, that land where the grafters thrive, but where, thank God, their day seems to be nearing an end. Mr. Blue was brought down here, and what has been the result ? The published reports of the province of Ontario are printed by a private concern, on the ordinary terms on which business is done by the Ontario government, without tender ; and, of course, the greater number of reports published, the greater the profit to those party friends who publish the reports ; so any one can understand that they print any number of them. In every one of these reports we see the name of Mr. Blue, and when it was known what salary he was to have, one can imagine the feeling of envy that ran through the mind of every Ontario official. Then if the hon. minister will look at the names of those who are engaged as enumerators, more particularly in Ontario, he will find

there his old friends, the Ontario government heelers. Take the riding of East Simeoe, where the cost of taking the census is simply enormous, when I look at the names of the grafters who got in their work there, I can congratulate him in getting off so safely. Are there any complaints of non-payment to the enumerators by the officers in charge ?
I am not aware of any.

I am glad that these sub-enumerators got their money paid to them at last. Politically, these sub-enumerators have done the government no good in East Simeoe because they complained that they could not get paid. In 1891 the cost of taking the census in East Simeoe was $5,473, and in 1901 it was $10,949.	1
find there were two enumerators appointed there at a total of $614, where in the previous census there was only one and the cost $386. How many ridings in the province of Ontario had government commissioners appointed in order that the government might reward its political heelers ?
I am not aware of any who were appointed for any such reason.
Why was Mr. Duncan McNab allowed $13.50 for horse-hire at $1.50 a day for the town of Orillia ?
Ir. some cases the enumerators charged horse-hire when they went to get their instructions. If that was not the reason, I cannot give any reason.

I can give the lion. Minister the real reason. Mr. McNab is a very warm political friend of hon. gentlemen opposite, now engaged in the Public Works Department in connection with a work going on in the riding. I notice that Mr. J. B. Henderson did not get any bore-hire. Yet he is a very important portion of the party machine. It will afford amusement to the people of East Simeoe to find that Mr. Henderson, in his innocence, did not put in a claim for horse-hire, while Mr. McNab sends in his bill for $13.50. What member of the hon. gentleman's staff directed to whom these allowances should be made for horse-hire ?
They were made on a well defined principle, and the commissioners for each locality had to certify the bills.

I am glad to have the hon. 'gentleman's statement. But what instructions were given by the commisssion-ers to the enumerators on this subject. I would like to have something in my hand by which to go to the electors of East Simeoe when I discuss this question.
No instructions except that the commissioners were given latitude, and were to certify the account.

If you take these- accounts all through you will find that wherever the political party hacks were at work they got all the allowances, whereas the man who was merely attending to the work of enumerating got little or nothing. Has the schedule been completed showing the return of crops ?
The compilation has not been completed. We hope it will be completed about the middle of next month.

With regard to the schedule for manufacturers, the effect of the change the hon. minister has made has apparently been disastrous to the flour industry. Ten years ago there were a number of flour mills in practically every riding in Ontario. But it is a large flour mill that employs five men, so many flour mills have been left unenumerated. One comparing this census with that of 1891 would suppose that the number of flour mills in Ontario had greatly decreased. Can the hon. gentleman tell what will be the effect of the method of taking the census upon the showing of the flour mills of Ontario 1
The compilation is not yet completed.

I hope the hon. minister will be able to give us some pertinent information next week when we go on with this item, because such an interesting item we cannot hope to dispose of at this forenoon session. I may say in passing the advantage is going to be taken of hon. gentlemen who are not present because the hon. leader of the House has not given notice that there would be a sitting to-day and consequently hon. gentlemen who are absent will not have an opportunity of taking part in this discussion.

I think the suggestion is calculated to bring us all to serious reflection. There are two large items remaining on this page of the estimates, and I am going to suggest to the hon. Minister of Agriculture that we should agree, if the committee are willing, that we should reserve the remaining discussion of the the census item and take the other items remaining on the page-that is item No. 56. That will clear up that page of the estimates except the census.
That stands ?
That would have to stand, of course.

I think that would be a reasonable suggestion at this hour. Possibly it might have been reasonable at an earlier hour, but we will not say anything about that. The only stipu-

lation I would like to make is that, if we pass the next item, and as there cannot be very much discussion now if we are going to have any breakfast, anything that would be open for discussion under that item shall be open for discussion either under the census item or some other convenient item.

Certainly.
Item No. 52 allowed to stand.
For the branch of the Commissioner of Agriculture and dairying, including live stock, dairy, bold storage, extension of markets, poultry, seed and fruit divisions ; employees' pay from this sum not to be subject to the Civil Service Act, $220,000.
The hon. Minister of Agriculture might just briefly explain the increase of $10,000 if it is convenient.

This is due to some enlargement of the work in connection with what I may call the outside markets division in connection with the sale of our goods in the old country. This has been pretty successful but there seems to be an opportunity of increasing the market.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
Might I ask what business will be taken up on Monday.

We will take up the consideration of the Patent Act, The Diseases of Animals Act, perhaps the Criminal Code, the Bill concerning Dry Docks and the Bill Respecting the Good Shepherds. I do not anticipate that on any of these Bills there is likely to be very much debate, and if not we will have time to resume the consideration of the Railway Committee Bill. If we reach Supply we will continue with the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture.
Better not start too late.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 6.20 a.m- Saturday.
Monday, June 15, 1903.
